entries.meaning: worthy of or causing disgrace.
examples: It is shameful to treat animals with such cruelty.
The politician's behaviour was described as shameful by the media.
It would be shameful to give up now after all our hard work.
He felt shameful about the lie he had told his parents.
The waste of food in this country is absolutely shameful.

entries.meaning: to set something on fire. To light, arouse or inspire.
examples: We used dry twigs to kindle the campfire.
Her stories helped to kindle an interest in history among the children.
The teacher hoped to kindle a love of reading in his students.
The sunset seemed to kindle the clouds with a golden glow.
A chance meeting helped to kindle their old friendship.

entries.meaning: ascertain the size, amount or degree of something. A standard unit.
examples: Please measure the length of the table before we buy the tablecloth.
The tailor needs to measure you for your new suit.
We must take measures to ensure the safety of the children.
It is difficult to measure the success of the project so early on.
The thermometer is used to measure the temperature of the room.

entries.meaning: movement of vehicles, ships, trains, aircraft or people.
examples: We were stuck in heavy traffic for over two hours.
The new bypass was built to reduce traffic in the town centre.
Air traffic controllers manage the movement of planes at the airport.
There is a lot of pedestrian traffic on the high street on Saturdays.
The bridge was closed to all traffic during the storm.

entries.meaning: relating to water. Growing or living in water.
examples: The aquarium has a wonderful display of aquatic plants and animals.
Dolphins are highly intelligent aquatic mammals.
We enjoyed watching the aquatic displays at the water park.
Some insects spend the first part of their lives as aquatic larvae.
Rice is an example of an aquatic crop that grows in flooded fields.

entries.meaning: lack of success. Not meeting a target.
examples: The experiment was a failure, but the scientists learned a lot from it.
He was afraid of failure and didn't want to try anything new.
The engine failure caused the car to stop in the middle of the road.
A failure to follow the rules will result in a punishment.
Despite their best efforts, the mission ended in failure.

entries.meaning: three of something. To multiply by three.
examples: She made a triple jump to win the gold medal.
The company hopes to triple its profits by next year.
He ordered a triple scoop of chocolate ice cream.
The noise was a triple threat to our concentration.
We need to triple the recipe to feed all the guests.

entries.meaning: change a gas or vapour into a liquid. To make something denser. To shorten.
examples: You can see the steam condense on the cold window pane.
The editor asked the author to condense the long novel.
We need to condense the main points of the meeting into a short report.
Adding milk will help to condense the thick soup.
The cold air caused the moisture in the breath to condense.

entries.meaning: a signature. Usually from someone famous.
examples: The fans waited outside the stadium to get the footballer's autograph.
She has a book full of autographs from famous actors.
He was kind enough to sign an autograph for the young boy.
The author signed an autograph on the front page of her new book.
I would love to have an autograph from my favourite singer.

entries.meaning: a follow-up work of art. A film or book that forms the next part of the story.
examples: The fans are eagerly waiting for the sequel to the hit movie.
The second book in the series is a direct sequel to the first one.
Most people thought the sequel was even better than the original film.
The story concludes in the long-awaited sequel.
The director is already planning a sequel to his latest project.

entries.meaning: a long narrow strip of something.
examples: She tied a blue ribbon in her hair.
The gift was wrapped in beautiful paper and tied with a silk ribbon.
The winning horse was decorated with a red ribbon.
A long ribbon of smoke rose from the chimney.
They cut the ribbon to officially open the new school building.

entries.meaning: the study of the physical or natural world through observations or experiments.
examples: Science helps us to understand how the world around us works.
She wants to study science at university and become a doctor.
We performed a fascinating experiment in our science lesson today.
Advances in science have led to many life-saving medical treatments.
Space exploration is one of the most exciting branches of science.

entries.meaning: the point or place where something starts, begins or comes from.
examples: The river has its origin in the high mountains.
Scientists are still researching the origin of the universe.
The word 'vocabulary' has its origin in Latin.
He is proud of his Irish origins.
The custom has its origins in an ancient festival.

entries.meaning: a transparent optical material that either concentrates or disperses light.
examples: The photographer cleaned the lens of his camera before taking the picture.
He needs new lenses for his glasses because his eyesight has changed.
A magnifying glass uses a special lens to make objects look larger.
The telescope has a powerful lens that allows us to see distant stars.
I accidentally scratched the lens of my sunglasses.

entries.meaning: an event that is sudden or striking. Exciting or impressive. Theatrical.
examples: The team scored a dramatic last-minute winner.
There was a dramatic improvement in his grades after he started studying.
The landscape changed dramatically as we drove from the mountains to the coast.
She has a very dramatic way of telling stories.
The play ended with a dramatic and unexpected twist.

entries.meaning: the first version of a piece of writing. To prepare a first version.
examples: I've written a first draft of my essay, but it needs a lot of work.
The architect showed them the draft plans for their new house.
He was asked to draft a letter to the council.
This is just a rough draft; I'll send you the final version tomorrow.
The constitution was drafted by a committee of experts.

entries.meaning: a person who sees an event (usually a crime). To see an event happen.
examples: The police are appealing for any witness to the accident to come forward.
She was called as a witness in the court case.
I was lucky enough to witness the birth of my nephew.
He was the sole witness to the robbery.
The document must be signed in the presence of a witness.

entries.meaning: to protect something/someone. Could be from heat loss, electricity or bad things.
examples: We need to insulate our loft to save money on our heating bills.
The wires were insulated with a rubber coating to prevent electric shocks.
He tried to insulate his children from the harsh realities of the world.
A wetsuit helps to insulate a diver from the cold water.
The flask is designed to insulate the contents and keep them hot.

entries.meaning: Threatening behaviour. The presence of danger.
examples: The dog gave a low, menacing growl.
The dark, menacing clouds warned of an approaching storm.
He had a menacing look in his eyes that frightened her.
The gang of youths looked menacing as they walked towards them.
The silence in the old house was more menacing than any noise.

entries.meaning: Serious, calm and in control. Worthy of respect.
examples: She remained dignified and calm despite the chaos around her.
The old professor had a very dignified and scholarly appearance.
He gave a dignified speech, accepting his defeat with grace.
Even when she was angry, she tried to behave in a dignified manner.
The queen walked with a dignified and royal air.

entries.meaning: a large and impressive building. An official residence (could be royal or a ruler etc).
examples: Buckingham Palace is the official residence of the Queen.
The tour took us through the magnificent state rooms of the palace.
The ancient palace was now a ruin, but you could still see its former glory.
The wealthy sheikh built a modern palace in the desert.
She felt like a princess when she visited the beautiful palace.

entries.meaning: the way in which two or more things are connected. Could be people or objects.
examples: It is important to have a good relationship with your friends and family.
The police are investigating the relationship between the two suspects.
There is a close relationship between poverty and crime.
He has a difficult relationship with his father.
The relationship between the two countries has improved in recent years.

entries.meaning: allowing or accepting what happens without resistance.
examples: He is too passive and lets other people make decisions for him.
She plays a very passive role in the team and rarely gets involved.
Passive smoking can be very harmful to your health.
The passive boy never stood up for himself.
Passive resistance was used to protest against the new law.

entries.meaning: to use up completely. Make someone feel tired. Expel gas or steam.
examples: The long hike up the mountain will exhaust even the fittest climbers.
We must not exhaust our natural resources before we find alternatives.
The car's tailpipe will exhaust harmful gases into the atmosphere.
If you don't take a break, you will exhaust yourself completely.
The athlete gave everything he had until he was exhausted.

entries.meaning: Causing great pain (physical or mental).
examples: He suffered an agonising injury during the football match.
Waiting for the exam results was an agonising experience.
She had to make the agonising decision to put her old dog to sleep.
The last few miles of the marathon were agonising.
He let out an agonising groan of pain.

entries.meaning: The highest, supreme, best. Happens at the end of a process.
examples: The ultimate prize for any footballer is to win the World Cup.
His ultimate ambition is to become a famous actor.
The ultimate decision rests with the manager.
This is the ultimate guide to cooking Italian food.
The ultimate fate of the universe is a mystery.

entries.meaning: the place where something or someone is.
examples: The police are trying to discover the whereabouts of the missing person.
His whereabouts are currently unknown.
Do you know the whereabouts of my keys? I can't find them anywhere.
She was last seen in the whereabouts of the old library.
The tracker allows us to know the whereabouts of the delivery van at all times.

entries.meaning: pleased, contented, happy.
examples: I am very satisfied with the quality of my new phone.
The teacher was not satisfied with his student's work.
He gave a satisfied smile after finishing the delicious meal.
She will not be satisfied until she gets a full refund.
Are you satisfied with the service you have received?

entries.meaning: an elaborated musical composition for an orchestra.
examples: We listened to a beautiful symphony by Mozart at the concert hall.
The orchestra performed Beethoven's famous 5th Symphony.
A symphony is usually composed of four separate movements.
The sound of the birds in the morning was like a symphony of nature.
He is composing a new symphony for the city's orchestra.

entries.meaning: alter or move something slightly. Adapting to a new situation.
examples: You can adjust the height of the chair to make it more comfortable.
It took him a while to adjust to his new school.
The driver had to adjust his mirrors before setting off.
I need to adjust my watch; it's five minutes fast.
She found it hard to adjust to living in a new country.

entries.meaning: decayed material used for fertiliser. To make compost.
examples: We make our own compost from vegetable peelings and grass cuttings.
Mixing compost into the soil will help your plants to grow.
You can buy bags of compost from the garden centre.
It is better for the environment to compost your food waste.
The council has a special collection for garden compost.

entries.meaning: a period of time set aside for an activity. An official meeting.
examples: I have a training session with the football team this evening.
The band booked a recording session at the music studio.
The parliament will hold a special session to debate the new law.
How many sessions of therapy have you had?
After a long study session, he took a well-deserved break.

entries.meaning: Dislike or feeling that a person or thing is worthless. Disrespectful of the law.
examples: He looked at his rival with utter contempt.
She has a deep contempt for people who are cruel to animals.
The politician was held in contempt by the public after the scandal.
He was found guilty of contempt of court for refusing to answer the judge's questions.
They treated his suggestion with contempt and laughed at him.

entries.meaning: a current of cold air.
examples: Can you close the door? There's a cold draught in here.
We sat by the fire to keep warm from the draughty old house.
Draught excluders can help to keep your home warm in winter.
She felt a draught on her back and shivered.
The candle flickered in the draught from the open window.

entries.meaning: Becoming aware of something. Understanding.
examples: I perceive a slight change in his attitude towards me.
Cats are able to perceive sounds that humans cannot hear.
How do you perceive the situation?
The new manager was perceived as being too strict.
She is not as confident as she is often perceived to be.

entries.meaning: nibble, chew or bite something.
examples: The dog was happily gnawing on a large bone.
The mouse had gnawed a hole in the skirting board.
He would often gnaw his pen when he was thinking.
The problem gnawed at her conscience and she couldn't sleep.
The hungry prisoner started to gnaw on a crust of bread.

entries.meaning: awake and aware of your surroundings.
examples: He was knocked over, but he remained conscious.
She made a conscious decision to eat more healthily.
I became conscious that someone was watching me.
He is very fashion-conscious and always wears the latest styles.
It is important to be conscious of the environment.

entries.meaning: to plan or invent.
examples: The team had to devise a new strategy to win the game.
He devised a clever plan to escape from the prison.
They are trying to devise a way to reduce traffic in the city centre.
The engineer devised a new machine to sort the letters.
She devised a system for keeping her files organised.

entries.meaning: a grain used for food. A breakfast food.
examples: I usually have a bowl of cereal for breakfast.
Wheat, rice, and corn are all types of cereal.
The farmer grows several different cereal crops on his farm.
Many breakfast cereals are fortified with vitamins and minerals.
My favourite cereal is cornflakes with milk and sugar.

entries.meaning: Spiteful, intending to harm.
examples: He was the victim of a malicious rumour that was intended to ruin his reputation.
The computer was infected with a malicious virus.
She gave him a malicious smile, and he knew she was up to no good.
He was found guilty of malicious damage after he deliberately broke the window.
Don't listen to her; she's just being malicious.

entries.meaning: able to endure (pain etc), fairly good (food etc).
examples: The pain was barely tolerable, but she tried not to complain.
The film was not great, but it was tolerable.
The conditions in the refugee camp were barely tolerable.
I find his arrogance just about tolerable.
The food in the canteen is tolerable, but it's not very exciting.

entries.meaning: being self-sufficient, free at liberty.
examples: The country fought for its independence from colonial rule.
Moving away from home gave her a new sense of independence.
Financial independence is very important to many people.
The Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776.
He is a very independent person and doesn't like to ask for help.

entries.meaning: a large group of animals. To move a group of animals.
examples: A herd of cows was grazing peacefully in the field.
We saw a large herd of elephants on our safari trip.
The farmer used his dog to herd the sheep into the pen.
It's not a good idea to just follow the herd; you should think for yourself.
They had to herd the children onto the bus.

entries.meaning: complying with an order or request.
examples: He was a very obedient child and always did what he was told.
My dog is very obedient and comes back when I call him.
The soldiers were expected to be completely obedient to their commanding officer.
The students were not very obedient and a lot of them were misbehaving.
She was an obedient and hardworking employee.

entries.meaning: Formal, dignified. Not cheerful, sad.
examples: He took a solemn oath to tell the truth in court.
The funeral was a solemn occasion.
She had a solemn expression on her face and didn't smile.
The room was filled with a solemn silence.
The wedding was a solemn and beautiful ceremony.

entries.meaning: a branch on a tree.
examples: The birds were singing on the bough of the old apple tree.
He hung a swing from a strong bough.
The wind whistled through the bare boughs of the winter trees.
The cat was stuck on a high bough and couldn't get down.
They decorated the boughs of the Christmas tree with baubles and lights.

entries.meaning: allowing the opinions of others, though not always agreeing.
examples: It is important to be tolerant of people from different cultures and backgrounds.
She is very tolerant of her husband's bad habits.
The teacher was not very tolerant of students who were late.
We need to create a more tolerant and inclusive society.
Some plants are more tolerant of drought than others.

entries.meaning: your choice. Best alternative.
examples: What is your preference: tea or coffee?
He was given preference for the job because he had more experience.
I have a strong preference for classical music over pop music.
The seating arrangements were made according to the guests' preferences.
Do you have any dietary preferences?

entries.meaning: something designed for a particular purpose.
examples: A smartphone is a very clever device that can do many different things.
The bomb disposal expert carefully disarmed the explosive device.
He invented a device to help people with disabilities to communicate.
The new kitchen is full of the latest labour-saving devices.
A compass is a simple device for finding your direction.

entries.meaning: part of a work. Repeated behaviour.
examples: The new TV drama is a six-part serial.
Charles Dickens originally published his novels as serials in a magazine.
The police are hunting for a serial killer.
You can find the serial number of the product on the back of the box.
He is a serial offender who has been in and out of prison for years.

entries.meaning: perceive a sound using your ears. (Past tense of hear).
examples: I heard a strange noise coming from outside.
Have you heard the news about the election?
She spoke so quietly that I could barely hear what she said.
He was last heard of living in Australia.
I've never heard of that author before.

entries.meaning: considerable size, importance or wealth.
examples: He inherited a substantial amount of money from his grandfather.
The company made a substantial profit this year.
There is a substantial difference between the two proposals.
The new house is much more substantial than their old one.
She needs a substantial meal after all that exercise.

entries.meaning: to send someone for further action or review.
examples: The doctor gave me a referral to see a specialist.
We get most of our new business through referrals from existing customers.
The case was passed on to the police for referral.
You will need a referral from your GP to see a consultant.
The social worker made a referral to the child protection team.

entries.meaning: move from one place to another. (Past tense of transfer).
examples: He has been transferred to a new job in our Paris office.
The patient was transferred to a different hospital.
I transferred the money from my savings account to my current account.
The ownership of the property was transferred to the new buyer.
The data was transferred from the old computer to the new one.

entries.meaning: A member of your family or a relation.
examples: All her close kin came to the wedding.
He felt a strong sense of loyalty to his kin.
In some cultures, it is common to live with your extended kin.
He is my next of kin, so he will inherit everything I own.
The police had to inform the next of kin about the accident.

entries.meaning: A scarcity or lack of something.
examples: There is a dearth of good restaurants in this town.
The long drought led to a dearth of food in the region.
There is no dearth of information on the internet.
The team's main problem is a dearth of skilled players.
A dearth of evidence meant that the police could not press charges.

entries.meaning: cheerful, happy and friendly.
examples: He was a jovial man who was always telling jokes.
The party was a very jovial occasion.
She was in a jovial mood and was smiling at everyone.
Our host was a jovial and welcoming person.
The jovial atmosphere in the pub made everyone feel relaxed.

entries.meaning: Expensive-looking. Finest quality.
examples: They had a sumptuous meal at a very expensive restaurant.
The palace was decorated with sumptuous furnishings.
She wore a sumptuous velvet gown to the ball.
The hotel's breakfast buffet was a sumptuous feast.
He lived a sumptuous lifestyle with a private jet and a yacht.

entries.meaning: a person who changes loyalty or their mind easily.
examples: The weather is notoriously fickle at this time of year.
He is a fickle friend who will desert you when you need him most.
Public opinion can be very fickle.
The fickle football fans soon turned against their team after a few bad results.
She is very fickle and is always changing her mind about what she wants to do.

entries.meaning: Showing charm, talent. Followed by others.
examples: The politician had a great deal of charisma and was very popular with voters.
She is a very charismatic leader who inspires great loyalty.
He may not be the most handsome actor, but he has a certain charisma.
The pop star's charisma made him a favourite with the fans.
You need a lot of charisma to be a successful TV presenter.

entries.meaning: to say what will happen in the future.
examples: It is difficult to predict the weather accurately.
No one could have predicted the outcome of the election.
The company is predicting a big increase in profits this year.
She claims to be able to predict the future.
The experts predict that the new technology will change our lives.

entries.meaning: large or plump. Round or spherical.
examples: The rotund little man had a cheerful, red face.
The teapot had a pleasingly rotund shape.
He had a rotund belly that shook when he laughed.
Santa Claus is often depicted as a rotund and jolly figure.
The vase was filled with rotund, ripe tomatoes.

entries.meaning: too important/valuable to be changed.
examples: The weekend is a sacrosanct time for me to spend with my family.
The tradition is regarded as sacrosanct and has not been changed for hundreds of years.
The player's position in the team is not sacrosanct; he could be dropped if he doesn't play well.
The principle of free speech is not sacrosanct and has to be balanced against other rights.
For many people, their home is a sacrosanct place.

entries.meaning: to assign, divide up or share.
examples: The teacher will apportion the sweets among all the children in the class.
The blame for the accident was apportioned equally between the two drivers.
The charity will apportion the money to where it is most needed.
The land was apportioned among the farmer's three sons.
It is a difficult job to apportion the resources fairly.

entries.meaning: Criminal deception for financial gain.
examples: He was sent to prison for tax fraud.
The company was accused of committing a massive fraud.
Be wary of emails that ask for your bank details; it could be a fraud.
She was a victim of a credit card fraud.
The police have set up a special unit to investigate online fraud.

entries.meaning: Especially made. A one-off.
examples: He had a bespoke suit made by a Savile Row tailor.
The company offers a bespoke service to its clients.
She designs bespoke wedding dresses for wealthy customers.
The furniture was all bespoke and designed to fit the room perfectly.
The car has a bespoke interior made from the finest leather.

entries.meaning: rude and mean-spirited manner.
examples: It would be churlish to refuse his generous offer of help.
He is a rather churlish man who is not very popular with his colleagues.
I thought it was very churlish of him not to say thank you.
She gave him a churlish reply and turned her back on him.
Don't be so churlish; just say you're sorry.

entries.meaning: a label/tag that stays with someone. Visible sign of illness. Also part of a flower.
examples: There is still a social stigma attached to mental illness.
He was worried about the stigma of being an ex-prisoner.
We need to remove the stigma associated with poverty.
In the past, there was a stigma attached to being a single mother.
The stigma of the disease made it difficult for him to find work.

entries.meaning: to dislike intensely.
examples: I detest having to get up early in the morning.
The two brothers absolutely detest each other.
She detests the smell of cigarette smoke.
He detests all forms of cruelty to animals.
I detest people who are rude to waiters.

entries.meaning: courteous, kind and pleasant manner. Showing elegance.
examples: She is a very gracious hostess who always makes her guests feel welcome.
It was very gracious of him to thank me for my help.
He gave a gracious speech after winning the award.
The queen gave a gracious smile to the cheering crowd.
They live in a gracious old house in the country.

entries.meaning: to gather in a crowd.
examples: A large crowd began to congregate in the square.
The students were told not to congregate in the corridors.
The birds congregate in large flocks before migrating south.
People began to congregate around the TV screen to watch the match.
The police have the power to break up any large groups of people who congregate in the street.

entries.meaning: acting in a superior manner.
examples: He gave a supercilious smile and looked down his nose at us.
She has a very supercilious manner and treats everyone as if they are beneath her.
I found his supercilious attitude very annoying.
The waiter gave us a supercilious look when we complained about the food.
He is a supercilious and arrogant man who has very few friends.

entries.meaning: to copy or pretend.
examples: The computer program can simulate the effects of an earthquake.
The pilots train in a flight simulator to practice for emergencies.
He simulated a fall in order to win a penalty.
The new material can simulate the feel of real leather.
The actors tried to simulate the conditions of being in a war zone.

entries.meaning: over confidence.
examples: He had the temerity to ask for a pay rise after only being in the job for a week.
She had the temerity to call the judge a fool.
No one had the temerity to question the manager's decision.
I can't believe he had the temerity to lie to my face.
He had the temerity to suggest that he was a better player than the team captain.

entries.meaning: The state of being away from a place or person.
examples: His absence from school was noticed by the teacher.
The absence of sunlight made the room feel cold and gloomy.
She felt a deep sadness during her father's absence.
In the absence of any evidence, the case was dropped.
His frequent absence from practice annoyed the coach.

entries.meaning: To send someone away from a country or place.
examples: The king decided to banish the traitor from the kingdom.
She tried to banish all negative thoughts from her mind.
The tribe voted to banish him for breaking their sacred rules.
He was banished to a remote island for ten years.
The new law aimed to banish dangerous criminals from the city.

entries.meaning: A person who creates a sequence of steps and moves for a performance.
examples: The choreographer designed a stunning routine for the ballet.
She has worked as a choreographer for many West End musicals.
The choreographer spent weeks rehearsing the dancers for the show.
He is a famous choreographer known for his creative and bold style.
The choreographer asked the performers to practise the final scene again.

entries.meaning: A person's sense of right or wrong.
examples: His conscience told him that cheating on the test was wrong.
She had a guilty conscience after lying to her parents.
He could not in good conscience ignore the suffering around him.
Her conscience would not allow her to keep the money she had found.
A clear conscience is the best pillow for a good night's sleep.

entries.meaning: A state of disorganisation or untidiness.
examples: The room was in complete disarray after the party.
The sudden resignation left the company in disarray.
Papers and books lay in disarray across the desk.
The army was thrown into disarray by the surprise attack.
She tried to bring some order to the disarray in the kitchen.

entries.meaning: To suffer something painful or difficult patiently.
examples: The explorers had to endure freezing temperatures during the expedition.
She endured months of pain before her injury healed.
He could not endure the long and boring lecture any longer.
The old bridge has endured centuries of storms and floods.
They endured many hardships before finally reaching safety.

entries.meaning: Not often or common.
examples: She seldom goes out on school nights.
He seldom eats fast food because he prefers home-cooked meals.
Snow seldom falls in this part of the country.
They seldom argue because they get along very well.
The old library is seldom visited by anyone these days.

entries.meaning: To express to someone your strong official disapproval of them.
examples: The teacher reprimanded the student for talking during the lesson.
He was reprimanded by his boss for arriving late to work.
The captain reprimanded the soldiers for not following orders.
She received a formal reprimand for her unprofessional behaviour.
The headmaster reprimanded the children for running in the corridor.

entries.meaning: Determined to do what he or she wants and refuses to do anything else.
examples: The stubborn mule refused to move no matter how hard they pulled.
She is very stubborn and never changes her mind once it is made up.
His stubborn attitude made it difficult to reach an agreement.
The stubborn stain on the carpet would not come out despite scrubbing.
He was too stubborn to ask for help even when he needed it.

entries.meaning: To voluntarily leave a job or office.
examples: The manager decided to resign after the team's poor results.
She resigned from her position to spend more time with her family.
He was forced to resign after the scandal became public.
The prime minister resigned and a new leader was elected.
She resigned from the committee because she disagreed with the new rules.

entries.meaning: To buy or obtain something.
examples: The school managed to procure new computers for the IT department.
It was difficult to procure fresh supplies during the winter.
She procured the rare book from a second-hand bookshop.
The charity worked hard to procure funding for the project.
He managed to procure tickets for the sold-out concert.

entries.meaning: A place for the storage of large quantities of something that are later dispatched.
examples: The delivery trucks picked up their packages from the depot every morning.
A large food depot was set up to supply aid to the refugees.
The bus depot is located on the edge of the town.
Weapons and ammunition were kept in a secure military depot.
The workers loaded the goods at the depot before the lorries set off.

entries.meaning: Puzzled, confused.
examples: He looked bemused when the magician made the coin disappear.
The students were bemused by the complicated maths problem.
She gave a bemused smile, unsure of what was going on.
The tourists stood bemused, trying to read the foreign signs.
He was left bemused by the sudden change in plans.

entries.meaning: To stick fast to a surface or substance.
examples: The glue made the label adhere firmly to the jar.
You must adhere to the school rules at all times.
The paint did not adhere well to the damp wall.
Everyone is expected to adhere to the dress code.
The sticker would not adhere to the wet surface.

entries.meaning: To steal goods from a place or person.
examples: The pirates sailed across the ocean to plunder merchant ships.
The invading army plundered the village and took everything of value.
The thieves plundered the museum of its most precious artefacts.
Ancient tombs were often plundered by treasure hunters.
The bandits plundered the travellers' belongings and disappeared into the forest.

entries.meaning: Responsible by law, at fault.
examples: The company was found liable for the damage caused by the faulty product.
If you break the window, you will be held liable for the cost of repair.
Parents are liable for the actions of their children.
The driver was liable for the accident because he ran a red light.
Anyone caught trespassing is liable to be prosecuted.

entries.meaning: To buy or obtain for oneself.
examples: She worked hard to acquire the skills needed for the job.
The museum acquired a rare painting from a private collector.
He acquired a taste for spicy food after travelling to India.
The company plans to acquire a smaller business to expand its reach.
It takes years to acquire fluency in a new language.

entries.meaning: A person who pretends to be shy but really is not.
examples: She gave a coy smile when asked about her plans for the weekend.
He was being coy about how much the present had cost.
The actress acted coy when reporters asked about her new film.
Stop being so coy and just tell us the answer!
She gave a coy wave as she walked onto the stage.

entries.meaning: Showing a rude and arrogant manner, lack of respect.
examples: The insolent boy refused to apologise for his rude behaviour.
She was sent out of class for her insolent remarks to the teacher.
His insolent tone made everyone in the room uncomfortable.
The manager dismissed the employee for his insolent attitude.
It is insolent to speak to your elders in such a disrespectful way.

entries.meaning: To try hard to do or achieve something.
examples: We must endeavour to finish the project before the deadline.
She always endeavours to do her best in every exam.
The team will endeavour to win the championship this year.
He endeavoured to learn three new words every day.
The charity endeavours to help those who are less fortunate.

entries.meaning: Of very great extent or quantity; immense.
examples: The Sahara Desert is a vast expanse of sand and rock.
There is a vast difference between the two proposals.
The ship sailed across the vast ocean for many weeks.
She inherited a vast fortune from her grandmother.
The library contains a vast collection of rare books.

entries.meaning: To prevent someone from doing something.
examples: The police had to restrain the angry crowd from pushing forward.
She tried to restrain her laughter during the serious meeting.
He could barely restrain his excitement when he heard the news.
The guard restrained the man from entering the building.
You must restrain your dog when walking near the road.

entries.meaning: The state of being separated from others.
examples: The patient was kept in isolation to prevent the spread of infection.
Living in isolation on the island made him feel very lonely.
The village's isolation meant that supplies were difficult to deliver.
She worked in isolation for months to finish her novel.
The long period of isolation during the winter was hard for the whole family.

entries.meaning: Without any imperfections or defects.
examples: The gymnast delivered a flawless routine and scored full marks.
Her flawless skin glowed in the sunlight.
The diamond was completely flawless and worth a fortune.
He gave a flawless performance on the piano at the concert.
The plan was executed in a flawless manner with no mistakes at all.

entries.meaning: To restrain or keep in check.
examples: The government introduced new laws to curb pollution.
She had to curb her spending after losing her job.
He tried to curb his temper when dealing with difficult customers.
The school took steps to curb bullying among the pupils.
New speed limits were introduced to curb dangerous driving.

entries.meaning: Untidy, disordered in appearance.
examples: He arrived at the interview looking dishevelled after running to catch the bus.
Her hair was dishevelled from playing outside in the wind.
The dishevelled man looked as though he had not slept in days.
After the long flight, the passengers looked tired and dishevelled.
She smoothed down her dishevelled clothes before entering the room.

entries.meaning: Not fit or suitable for eating.
examples: The berries growing in the hedge are bright red but completely inedible.
The burnt toast was dry and inedible.
Some wild mushrooms are inedible and can be very poisonous.
After being left out for days, the food became inedible.
The cake she baked was rock-hard and inedible.

entries.meaning: To satisfy thirst by drinking.
examples: After the long run, she drank a large glass of water to quench her thirst.
Nothing could quench his thirst on that scorching summer day.
The firefighters worked through the night to quench the blaze.
He gulped down the cold lemonade to quench his thirst.
A single sip of water was not enough to quench her thirst after the hike.

entries.meaning: Pieces of information of little importance or value.
examples: The quiz night was full of fun trivia questions about history and science.
He loves collecting trivia about his favourite football team.
The book is packed with fascinating trivia about the animal kingdom.
She is brilliant at trivia and always wins the pub quiz.
Don't waste your time on trivia when you have important work to do.

entries.meaning: Rather fat or of a heavy build.
examples: The stout gentleman struggled to fit into the narrow seat.
She was a stout woman with a kind face and a warm smile.
He pulled on a stout pair of walking boots before heading out.
The table was supported by four stout wooden legs.
Despite his stout frame, he was surprisingly quick on his feet.

entries.meaning: A position within a grading system.
examples: She held the rank of captain in the army.
The school was given the highest rank in the country for its exam results.
He rose through the ranks to become the head of the company.
Students were listed in rank order according to their test scores.
The officer was promoted to the rank of sergeant after years of service.

entries.meaning: The natural colouring of animal or plant tissue.
examples: Melanin is the pigment that gives human skin its colour.
The artist mixed different pigments to create the perfect shade of blue.
Some animals can change the pigment in their skin to blend in with their surroundings.
The leaves lose their green pigment in autumn and turn red and gold.
Ancient cave paintings were made using natural pigments from the earth.

entries.meaning: Feeling inclined to vomit.
examples: The bumpy car ride made her feel nauseous.
He felt nauseous after eating too much chocolate.
The strong smell of paint made everyone in the room feel nauseous.
She was nauseous with nerves before the big exam.
The passengers on the boat began to feel nauseous as the waves grew larger.

entries.meaning: To express complete disapproval of something.
examples: The prime minister condemned the attack and called for peace.
Many people condemned the decision to close the local hospital.
The judge condemned the criminal to ten years in prison.
Human rights groups condemned the treatment of the prisoners.
The building was condemned as unsafe and no one was allowed to enter.

entries.meaning: Comically or repulsively ugly or distorted.
examples: The gargoyles on the cathedral had grotesque faces carved in stone.
The mask he wore for Halloween was truly grotesque.
The villain in the story was described as a grotesque figure lurking in the shadows.
She found the painting grotesque and could not bear to look at it.
The old tree had grown into a grotesque shape over the years.

entries.meaning: A trick intended to deceive someone.
examples: The bomb threat turned out to be a hoax.
The photograph of the monster was later revealed to be a hoax.
Someone played a cruel hoax on the family by sending a fake letter.
The email claiming she had won a prize was nothing but a hoax.
The police warned people not to fall for the online hoax.

entries.meaning: Made aware of or familiar with something or someone.
examples: Are you acquainted with the rules of the game?
She became acquainted with her new neighbours at the street party.
He is well acquainted with the history of the town.
The teacher made sure the new students were acquainted with the school layout.
They first became acquainted when they worked together on a project.

entries.meaning: To expose someone to danger by being disloyal or treacherous.
examples: He promised never to betray his friend's secret.
The spy was caught trying to betray his country.
She felt hurt when her best friend betrayed her trust.
The soldier refused to betray his comrades even under pressure.
His nervous expression betrayed the fact that he was lying.

entries.meaning: Someone that a person spends a lot of time with.
examples: The dog has been her faithful companion for over ten years.
He made a good travelling companion because he was always cheerful.
She hired a companion to keep her grandmother company during the day.
The two boys became close companions after meeting at school.
A good book can be a wonderful companion on a long journey.

entries.meaning: Certain or sure about something.
examples: We need a definite answer by Friday.
There has been a definite improvement in her behaviour this term.
It is definite that the match will take place on Saturday.
He had no definite plans for the summer holidays.
The teacher gave definite instructions about how to complete the task.

entries.meaning: Severe physical or mental suffering.
examples: The long wait for the exam results was sheer torment.
He was in torment after losing his beloved pet.
The mosquitoes tormented the campers throughout the night.
She could not hide the torment she felt after the argument.
The memory of his mistake continued to torment him for weeks.

entries.meaning: Strongly and solidly built.
examples: The sturdy oak table had been in the family for generations.
He wore a pair of sturdy boots for the mountain hike.
The bridge looked old but was still surprisingly sturdy.
She chose a sturdy backpack that could carry all her books.
The sturdy little pony carried the children safely up the hill.

entries.meaning: Showing genuine feeling; free from pretence or deceit.
examples: She gave a sincere apology for breaking the vase.
His sincere smile made everyone feel welcome at the party.
The teacher appreciated the student's sincere effort to improve.
He made a sincere promise to help his friend with the project.
Her sincere words of encouragement lifted his spirits before the race.

entries.meaning: A solemn promise or undertaking.
examples: The scouts made a pledge to keep the park clean.
She pledged to practise the piano every day before the concert.
The charity received a generous pledge of support from the company.
He gave his pledge that he would never reveal the secret.
The new members pledged their loyalty to the team.

entries.meaning: Make someone do something through reasoning or argument.
examples: She tried to persuade her parents to let her go to the sleepover.
The salesman persuaded him to buy the more expensive model.
It took a long time to persuade the cat to come down from the tree.
He persuaded his friend to join the football team.
Nothing could persuade her to change her mind about the trip.

entries.meaning: A solemn promise, often calling upon God or a sacred object as witness.
examples: The witness took an oath to tell the truth in court.
The knight swore an oath of loyalty to the king.
Doctors take an oath to care for their patients.
He broke his oath by revealing the secret to others.
The new president took the oath of office in front of thousands.

entries.meaning: Quick and light in movement.
examples: The nimble gymnast performed a perfect backflip.
The squirrel was nimble enough to leap between the branches.
Her nimble fingers flew across the piano keys.
You need to be nimble on your feet to play badminton well.
The nimble fox darted through the gap in the fence.

entries.meaning: Side by side and having the same distance continuously between them.
examples: The two railway lines ran parallel to each other for miles.
She drew two parallel lines across the page with a ruler.
The road runs parallel to the river through the valley.
The shelves were fixed parallel to the floor so nothing would slide off.
The teacher asked the class to find examples of parallel lines in the classroom.

entries.meaning: A distinctive smell, especially an unpleasant one.
examples: A strange odour was coming from the back of the fridge.
The odour of rotten eggs filled the science lab after the experiment.
She noticed an unpleasant odour as soon as she entered the room.
The bakery gave off a wonderful odour of freshly baked bread.
He wrinkled his nose at the foul odour drifting from the bin.

entries.meaning: Not discovered or known about; uncertain.
examples: The meaning of the ancient inscription remained obscure to the historians.
She found the book in an obscure corner of the library.
The path was obscured by thick fog and fallen leaves.
He quoted an obscure poet that nobody in the class had heard of.
The real reason for his absence remained obscure to his friends.

entries.meaning: To intervene in a situation without invitation or necessity.
examples: Please do not interfere while I am trying to concentrate on my work.
She asked her brother to stop interfering in her business.
The rain interfered with the school sports day plans.
He did not want to interfere in the argument between his friends.
The loud music from next door interfered with her revision.

entries.meaning: A shortage of food leading to extreme scarcity and hunger.
examples: The terrible famine forced many families to leave their village.
Crops failed for the third year, and famine spread across the region.
Charities worked hard to send food to the areas affected by famine.
The history lesson covered the great famine of the nineteenth century.
Without rain, the farmers feared that famine would follow.

entries.meaning: Permission for something to happen or agreement to do something.
examples: You must have your parents' consent before joining the school trip.
The teacher gave her consent for the class to use the library.
He would not consent to the plan without reading it first.
The council granted consent for the new playground to be built.
She signed a consent form before the medical procedure.

entries.meaning: To make new or secret information known.
examples: The detective refused to disclose the name of the witness.
She was not ready to disclose her surprise plans for the party.
The company was forced to disclose the results of the safety report.
He disclosed the secret hiding place to his best friend.
The letter disclosed important details about the treasure hunt.

entries.meaning: Extreme anxiety, sorrow, or pain.
examples: The lost child was clearly in great distress.
She could see the distress on his face when he heard the bad news.
The storm caused considerable distress to the coastal village.
He tried to hide his distress so as not to worry his family.
The animal charity rescues pets that are in distress.

entries.meaning: The state of being strikingly different from something else.
examples: The contrast between the two paintings was striking.
Her bright red coat stood out in sharp contrast to the snowy background.
The teacher asked the class to contrast life in the city with life in the countryside.
There was a clear contrast between his calm words and his angry expression.
In contrast to her brother, she preferred reading to playing sport.

entries.meaning: To represent something as being larger, better, or worse than it really is.
examples: He tends to exaggerate the size of the fish he catches.
She was accused of exaggerating how difficult the test had been.
Please do not exaggerate — just tell me exactly what happened.
The newspaper was criticised for exaggerating the danger of the storm.
It is hard to exaggerate how important this match is to the team.

entries.meaning: To protect something from harm or destruction; to use carefully.
examples: We must conserve water during the hot summer months.
The national park was created to conserve the local wildlife.
She tried to conserve her energy for the final lap of the race.
Turning off lights when you leave a room helps conserve electricity.
The charity works to conserve ancient buildings and monuments.

entries.meaning: Anxious or fearful that something bad or unpleasant will happen.
examples: She felt apprehensive about starting at a new school.
He was apprehensive before his first solo flight.
The children were apprehensive about walking through the dark forest.
Despite feeling apprehensive, she stepped onto the stage and began to sing.
The team was apprehensive ahead of the important final match.

entries.meaning: To bring or come to an end; to reach a judgement or opinion.
examples: The headteacher concluded the assembly with a few words of encouragement.
After examining the evidence, the detective concluded that the butler was innocent.
The concert concluded with a spectacular fireworks display.
She concluded her essay with a powerful closing statement.
We can conclude from the experiment that plants need sunlight to grow.

entries.meaning: Enough or more than enough; plentiful.
examples: There was ample food at the party for everyone to have seconds.
Make sure you allow ample time to finish the exam.
The garden provided ample space for the children to play.
She had ample reason to feel proud of her achievement.
The hotel room was ample enough for the whole family.

entries.meaning: A load, typically a heavy one; could be physical or mental.
examples: The donkey struggled under the burden of heavy sacks.
She did not want to burden her parents with her worries.
Carrying all the shopping bags up the hill was a real burden.
The burden of homework felt overwhelming before the exams.
He shared the burden of the chores equally with his sister.

entries.meaning: The way in which something is made up or put together.
examples: The teacher asked the class to write a composition about their holidays.
Scientists studied the composition of the rock samples from the cave.
The composition of the orchestra included strings, brass, and woodwind.
She admired the beautiful composition of the painting in the gallery.
The chemical composition of water is two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen.

entries.meaning: To prepare and use land for crops or gardening; to develop or improve something.
examples: The farmer worked hard to cultivate the dry, rocky land.
She cultivated a small vegetable patch in the back garden.
Reading widely will help you cultivate a love of language.
The villagers cultivated rice in the fields beside the river.
He tried to cultivate good habits such as reading before bed.

entries.meaning: To transport or carry to a place; to communicate a message or idea.
examples: The lorry was used to convey goods from the factory to the shop.
She tried to convey her feelings through a heartfelt letter.
The ambassador was sent to convey the government's message of peace.
A belt of rollers conveys the luggage to the aircraft.
His smile conveyed more than any words could have expressed.

entries.meaning: To feel contempt or deep dislike for someone or something.
examples: She despised bullies who picked on younger children.
He despised getting up early on cold winter mornings.
The villain was despised by everyone in the village.
She despised dishonesty and always told the truth.
Although they were rivals, he did not despise his opponent.

entries.meaning: A short journey undertaken in order to collect or deliver something.
examples: Mum sent me on an errand to buy milk from the corner shop.
He ran several errands for his grandmother after school.
She was happy to help by doing errands around the neighbourhood.
The errand took longer than expected because of the traffic.
Before the party, there were many errands to complete.

entries.meaning: To feel intense sorrow, especially after a loss.
examples: The whole school grieved when the beloved headteacher retired.
She grieved deeply for her grandfather who had passed away.
It is natural to grieve when you lose someone close to you.
The community grieved together after the terrible storm destroyed their homes.
He grieved the loss of his childhood home when it was demolished.

entries.meaning: Highly successful, authoritative, and commanding great respect.
examples: The distinguished professor was invited to give a lecture at the university.
She had a long and distinguished career in medicine.
The distinguished gentleman arrived at the ceremony in a fine suit.
He was a distinguished war hero who had served his country bravely.
The school welcomed several distinguished guests to its prize-giving evening.

entries.meaning: Not clearly visible or attracting attention; not easily noticed.
examples: The spy tried to remain inconspicuous by blending into the crowd.
She chose an inconspicuous seat at the back of the room.
The small, inconspicuous door led to a magnificent secret garden.
He wore plain clothes to be as inconspicuous as possible.
The camera was placed in an inconspicuous position on the shelf.

entries.meaning: A person or thing causing inconvenience or annoyance.
examples: The noisy roadworks outside the school were a real nuisance.
Flies buzzing around the kitchen were a terrible nuisance.
He made a nuisance of himself by constantly interrupting the lesson.
The broken gate was a nuisance because it let the dog escape.
She considered the long detour to be a great nuisance.

entries.meaning: To officially allow someone to do something; a document giving permission.
examples: The teacher did not permit talking during the exam.
You need a permit to fish in this lake.
The weather permitted the outdoor sports day to go ahead.
Visitors are not permitted to enter the building after six o'clock.
She applied for a permit to hold a market stall in the town square.

entries.meaning: To keep someone in subjection and hardship; to treat unfairly.
examples: The cruel ruler oppressed the people with heavy taxes.
Throughout history, many groups have been oppressed because of their beliefs.
She spoke out against those who oppressed the poor and vulnerable.
The workers felt oppressed by the unfair rules in the factory.
He fought to free the oppressed communities in his country.

entries.meaning: A special right or advantage granted to a particular person or group.
examples: It was a privilege to meet the famous author at the book signing.
Driving a car is a privilege, not a right, and must be earned.
The older students enjoyed the privilege of using the common room.
She never took for granted the privilege of a good education.
Being chosen as team captain was a great privilege.

entries.meaning: Occurring or situated nearer to the end of something than to the beginning.
examples: Of the two choices, she preferred the latter option.
The latter half of the film was much more exciting than the first.
He spent the latter part of his career teaching abroad.
Given the choice between cake and fruit, I would choose the latter.
In the latter stages of the race, she overtook three runners.

entries.meaning: To settle or find a solution to a problem; firm determination.
examples: The two friends resolved their argument with a calm discussion.
She resolved to work harder after receiving her report card.
The plumber was called to resolve the problem with the leaking pipe.
It took several meetings to resolve the dispute between the neighbours.
His resolve to finish the marathon kept him running despite the pain.

entries.meaning: To feel deep regret or remorse about one's wrongdoing.
examples: He repented his harsh words as soon as he saw her tears.
The character in the story repented his selfish behaviour and changed his ways.
She repented not studying harder when she saw her exam results.
It is never too late to repent and try to make things right.
He deeply repented breaking his promise to his best friend.

entries.meaning: Free from disturbance; calm and peaceful.
examples: The tranquil lake reflected the snow-capped mountains perfectly.
She found a tranquil spot under the oak tree to read her book.
The village was so tranquil that you could hear the birds singing.
After the storm, the sea became tranquil once more.
He longed for a tranquil weekend away from the busy city.

entries.meaning: Contrary to what is usual, traditional, or accepted.
examples: The scientist had an unorthodox approach to solving the problem.
Her unorthodox teaching methods made the lessons fun and memorable.
He held unorthodox views that often surprised his classmates.
The chef's unorthodox recipe combined chocolate with chilli peppers.
Although his style was unorthodox, the results spoke for themselves.

entries.meaning: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse.
examples: The weather in spring can be very volatile, changing from sun to rain in minutes.
The volatile situation in the playground required a teacher to step in.
Certain chemicals are volatile and must be handled with great care.
His volatile temper meant that people were careful around him.
The stock market became volatile after the unexpected announcement.

entries.meaning: Wildly unreasonable or illogical.
examples: It seemed absurd to carry an umbrella on such a bright, sunny day.
The idea that cats could fly is completely absurd.
She laughed at the absurd plot twist in the comedy film.
He made an absurd suggestion that they walk a hundred miles to save money.
The teacher found it absurd that the pupil had forgotten to bring a pencil three days in a row.

entries.meaning: Perplexed and confused; unable to understand something.
examples: The tourist looked bewildered as she tried to read the foreign map.
He was bewildered by the complicated maths problem on the board.
The young puppy appeared bewildered in its new home.
She felt bewildered when all her friends suddenly fell silent.
The bewildered boy had no idea why everyone was laughing.

entries.meaning: To keep something from being seen or known; to hide.
examples: The magician used a cloth to conceal the rabbit before the trick.
She tried to conceal her disappointment when she didn't win the prize.
The spy concealed the documents inside a false-bottomed briefcase.
Heavy clouds concealed the sun for most of the afternoon.
He found it hard to conceal his excitement about the birthday surprise.

entries.meaning: To make secret plans jointly to commit an unlawful or harmful act.
examples: The two villains conspired to steal the jewels from the museum.
It seemed as though everything conspired to make her day go wrong.
The boys were caught conspiring to cheat during the exam.
In the story, the advisors conspired against the king behind closed doors.
She suspected her colleagues were conspiring to keep a secret from her.

entries.meaning: To oppose or challenge an action or theory as wrong; also a competition.
examples: The losing team decided to contest the referee's final decision.
She entered a poetry contest and won first place.
The lawyer chose to contest the evidence presented in court.
Three candidates decided to contest the position of head boy.
He did not contest the result, even though he felt it was unfair.

entries.meaning: To cause someone to believe firmly in the truth of something.
examples: She managed to convince her parents to let her stay up late.
The salesman tried to convince us that his product was the best.
No one could convince him that he had made a mistake.
The scientist convinced the audience with her clear and detailed evidence.
He convinced his friend to try the new restaurant by describing the food.

entries.meaning: Getting what one wants in a clever, deceptive way.
examples: The cunning fox tricked the other animals into sharing their food.
She devised a cunning plan to escape the locked room.
The villain in the story was cunning enough to outwit the detective.
He used a cunning disguise to sneak into the party uninvited.
Despite being small, the cunning spider trapped much larger insects in its web.

entries.meaning: To give all or most of one's time or effort to a person or activity.
examples: She devoted her weekends to learning a new language.
The nurse devoted her career to caring for elderly patients.
He devotes at least an hour each evening to reading.
The charity devotes all of its funds to helping homeless children.
She devoted herself completely to practising for the piano recital.

entries.meaning: An enemy or opponent.
examples: In the legend, the brave knight faced his greatest foe alone.
The two politicians were long-standing foes who rarely agreed on anything.
The hero had to outsmart his foe to rescue the captured villagers.
Even in sport, it is important to respect your foe.
The two cats eyed each other as sworn foes until they slowly became friends.

entries.meaning: Unable to be heard.
examples: Her whisper was completely inaudible over the noise of the crowd.
The teacher asked the pupil to speak up as his answer was inaudible.
The bat uses inaudible sound waves to navigate in the dark.
From the back of the hall, the speaker's voice was almost inaudible.
She muttered something inaudible under her breath and walked away.

entries.meaning: A surgical cut made in skin or flesh.
examples: The surgeon made a small incision before removing the splinter.
The incision healed well after the operation.
A clean incision is important to reduce the risk of infection.
She wore a bandage over the incision to protect it.
The doctor explained that the incision would leave only a tiny scar.

entries.meaning: Of extreme force, degree, or strength.
examples: The intense heat of the desert sun made walking difficult.
She gave the maths problem intense concentration for twenty minutes.
The match was so intense that the crowd barely breathed.
He felt an intense sense of pride when his team won the trophy.
The intense colours of the sunset painted the sky in vivid shades.

entries.meaning: A disease or ailment.
examples: The doctor diagnosed a rare malady that required specialist treatment.
The whole village seemed to be suffering from the same malady.
Rest and fluids are the best cures for a mild malady.
She nursed her brother through a nasty malady that lasted two weeks.
The ancient text described a mysterious malady that struck the town.

entries.meaning: The way in which a word or language is pronounced.
examples: The teacher corrected the pupil's pronunciation of the word "February".
She listened to audio recordings to improve her French pronunciation.
Clear pronunciation helps the audience understand a speaker more easily.
He was embarrassed by his pronunciation of the difficult surname.
The pronunciation of many English words does not match their spelling.

entries.meaning: To tremble or shake with a slight, rapid motion.
examples: Her lips began to quiver just before she burst into tears.
The leaves quivered gently in the soft afternoon breeze.
His voice quivered with nerves as he stood up to speak.
The frightened puppy quivered in the corner of the room.
She felt her hands quiver as she opened the results envelope.

entries.meaning: To talk or write at length in a confused or inconsequential way; also to walk for leisure.
examples: The professor tended to ramble, making it hard to take clear notes.
They went for a long ramble through the countryside on Sunday morning.
She asked him to stop rambling and get to the point.
The old man would ramble on about his childhood for hours.
Try not to ramble in your essay — make each sentence count.

entries.meaning: To bring back or re-establish a previous right, situation, or condition.
examples: The team worked hard to restore the old painting to its original condition.
The peace treaty helped to restore calm to the troubled region.
She restored the deleted file from the recycling bin on her computer.
The gardener restored the overgrown garden to its former beauty.
The new headteacher restored trust by listening to pupils and parents.

entries.meaning: Of sound mind; not mad or mentally ill; sensible and rational.
examples: After days without sleep, she struggled to make sane decisions.
The doctor confirmed that the patient was perfectly sane.
He was the only sane voice in the chaotic meeting.
Keeping a daily routine helped her stay calm and sane during difficult times.
It seemed like the sane thing to do was to ask for help.

entries.meaning: Existing or occurring beneath the earth's surface.
examples: The explorers discovered a vast subterranean cave beneath the hillside.
Many cities have subterranean train networks that run beneath the streets.
The subterranean roots of the ancient tree stretched for metres in every direction.
Scientists found a subterranean river flowing deep beneath the desert.
The ant colony built an impressive subterranean network of tunnels.

entries.meaning: Moving unsteadily or violently; characterised by conflict or disorder.
examples: The turbulent river swept away anything in its path.
Passengers were asked to fasten their seatbelts during the turbulent flight.
It was a turbulent period in the country's history, full of protests and change.
The turbulent sea made it impossible for the fishing boats to leave harbour.
After a turbulent start to the season, the team finally found their form.

entries.meaning: Friendly and easy to talk to; pleasant in manner.
examples: The new teacher was so affable that pupils felt comfortable asking questions.
His affable manner made him popular with everyone in the office.
She was greeted by an affable shopkeeper who offered to help straight away.
Despite being famous, the author remained affable and chatted with all his fans.
An affable smile and a kind word can make a huge difference to someone's day.

entries.meaning: An event causing sudden and widespread damage or distress; a disaster.
examples: The flooding of the village was a terrible calamity for the local community.
Losing her passport the day before the trip felt like a complete calamity.
The earthquake was the worst calamity the region had experienced in decades.
Quick action by the firefighters prevented a calamity in the town centre.
The calamity brought the community together as people helped one another recover.

entries.meaning: To yearn to possess something belonging to another; to desire wrongfully.
examples: He coveted his neighbour's brand-new bicycle and dreamed of having one himself.
She tried not to covet the prizes her classmates had won.
The antique dealer coveted the rare painting he had seen at the auction.
It is wrong to covet what others have instead of being grateful for your own.
He openly coveted the captain's armband and trained hard to earn it.

entries.meaning: Rudely brief in manner or speech; abrupt.
examples: His curt reply made it clear he did not want to discuss the matter further.
She was surprised by the teacher's curt response to her question.
A curt nod was all she received when she said good morning to him.
He gave a curt answer of "no" without any explanation.
The manager's curt tone suggested she was unhappy with the team's performance.

entries.meaning: To deliberately cause someone to believe something that is not true.
examples: The dishonest trader tried to deceive customers about the quality of his goods.
She felt betrayed when she realised her friend had deceived her.
The magician's job is to deceive the audience in a fun and entertaining way.
He attempted to deceive his parents by pretending he had done his homework.
Appearances can often deceive — the quiet pupil turned out to be the most talented.

entries.meaning: Lacking money, food, or shelter; extremely poor.
examples: After the fire destroyed their home, the family was left completely destitute.
The charity raised money to help destitute families during the harsh winter.
He arrived in the city destitute, with nothing but the clothes on his back.
The flood left hundreds of villagers destitute and in need of urgent aid.
She volunteered at a shelter to help those who were destitute and homeless.

entries.meaning: Resulting from or showing sincere and intense conviction; serious in intention.
examples: She made an earnest promise to return the borrowed book by Friday.
His earnest expression showed that he truly meant every word he said.
The pupil made an earnest effort to improve after her teacher's feedback.
He was in earnest when he said he wanted to become a doctor one day.
The earnest young man stayed behind after class to ask for extra help.

entries.meaning: To force someone or something to leave a place; to officially remove someone.
examples: The school threatened to expel any pupil caught cheating in exams.
The diplomat was expelled from the country following the dispute.
He was expelled from the team after breaking the rules three times.
The volcano began to expel huge clouds of ash into the sky.
She feared she would be expelled from the competition for arriving late.

entries.meaning: To dip or submerge in a liquid; to involve oneself deeply in something.
examples: She immersed the vegetables in cold water to keep them fresh.
He immersed himself in his studies during the weeks before the exam.
The diver immersed himself fully before beginning to explore the reef.
She loved to immerse herself in a good book on rainy afternoons.
The cloth must be fully immersed in the dye for the colour to take properly.

entries.meaning: Not harmful or offensive; unlikely to cause any ill effects.
examples: What seemed like an innocuous comment upset her more than he had expected.
The spider found in the garden turned out to be completely innocuous.
He made an innocuous joke that everyone laughed at without taking offence.
The chemical was innocuous in small amounts but dangerous in large doses.
Her innocuous question accidentally revealed the surprise they had been planning.

entries.meaning: Sumptuously rich, elaborate, or luxurious; to give generously.
examples: The guests were treated to a lavish banquet with dozens of courses.
She decorated her home in a lavish style with gold and velvet furnishings.
He lavished praise on the pupils who had worked hardest during term.
The lavish hotel suite had a private pool and views over the city.
It was a lavish celebration, with fireworks, live music, and exotic food.

entries.meaning: Average in amount, intensity, or degree; neither very great nor very little.
examples: The doctor recommended moderate exercise, such as a daily walk.
Temperatures remained moderate throughout the spring half term.
She achieved moderate success in her first year of business.
A moderate amount of rain fell, which was enough to water the garden.
He ate a moderate portion rather than piling his plate high.

entries.meaning: To make someone legally or morally bound to do something; to do someone a favour.
examples: The new law obliges all drivers to wear a seatbelt at all times.
She felt obliged to help her neighbour carry the heavy shopping bags.
He was happy to oblige when his teacher asked him to read aloud.
The school is obliged to provide support for pupils with additional needs.
As the host, she felt obliged to make sure every guest was comfortable.

entries.meaning: To deliberately make someone annoyed or angry; to stimulate a reaction.
examples: He tried to provoke his sister by taking her favourite book without asking.
The politician's speech provoked an angry response from the crowd.
She knew better than to provoke the teacher with cheeky remarks.
The dog began to bark as if something outside had provoked it.
His deliberate attempts to provoke a reaction were ignored completely.

entries.meaning: To put an end to something, especially by using force; to suppress.
examples: The head teacher was called in to quell the argument in the playground.
She took a deep breath to quell her nerves before walking on stage.
The police were called to quell the disturbance outside the stadium.
He tried to quell his excitement so he would not spoil the surprise.
The captain's calm words were enough to quell the panic among the crew.

entries.meaning: To repeat something aloud from memory, especially before an audience.
examples: She stood up confidently to recite the poem she had learned that week.
The class was asked to recite their times tables at the start of the lesson.
He could recite the names of all the capital cities without hesitation.
She had practised enough times to recite the speech without any notes.
The children gathered around to recite the school's founding pledge together.

entries.meaning: A dishonest or unprincipled person; something that behaves in an erratic way.
examples: The rogue trader was arrested for selling counterfeit goods at the market.
In the story, the rogue used clever tricks to steal from unsuspecting travellers.
A rogue wave struck the boat without warning, sending water across the deck.
Despite being a loveable rogue, everyone knew he could not be fully trusted.
The rogue elephant had separated from its herd and was roaming the village.

entries.meaning: Relating to the conditions that affect hygiene and health; clean and hygienic.
examples: The kitchen must be kept sanitary to prevent the spread of germs.
Inspectors visited the restaurant to check that sanitary standards were being met.
She always carried hand sanitiser to keep her hands sanitary on the go.
The hospital introduced strict sanitary procedures to protect patients.
Clean water and sanitary conditions are essential for good public health.

entries.meaning: Very stormy; full of wild and conflicting emotions or forces.
examples: The sailors struggled to control the boat in the tempestuous sea.
Their tempestuous relationship was full of arguments followed by apologies.
The tempestuous weather made it impossible to hold the outdoor event.
Dark clouds rolled in, signalling the start of a tempestuous afternoon.
The tempestuous debate in parliament lasted well into the evening.

entries.meaning: In a very unhappy or unfortunate state; of very poor quality.
examples: She felt absolutely wretched when she realised she had hurt her friend's feelings.
The wretched conditions in the old building meant it had to be demolished.
He spent a wretched night tossing and turning, unable to sleep.
The wretched dog had been left outside in the rain without shelter.
Despite feeling wretched with a cold, she refused to miss the important match.

entries.meaning: To make someone accept something as normal or familiar through habit.
examples: It took a few weeks to accustom herself to waking up early for school.
The trainer helped the new recruits accustom themselves to the long marches.
Moving abroad meant the family had to accustom themselves to a new culture.
She quickly accustomed herself to the noise of the busy city centre.
It can take time to accustom your eyes to darkness after coming indoors.

entries.meaning: Showing great care, dedication, and perseverance in one's work.
examples: Her assiduous revision paid off when she achieved top marks in every subject.
The assiduous young scientist checked his results three times to be sure.
An assiduous worker, she never left the office before completing every task.
He was assiduous in practising the piano, never missing a single session.
The teacher praised the pupils for their assiduous effort throughout the term.

entries.meaning: To make a gesture with the hand to summon or signal someone.
examples: The librarian beckoned to the children to come and listen to the story.
She beckoned her friend over with a wave from across the playground.
The guide beckoned the group forward along the narrow mountain path.
He stood at the door and beckoned the visitor inside out of the rain.
The shopkeeper beckoned to the customer who was peering through the window.

entries.meaning: Surrounded or crowded in on all sides; overwhelmed with requests or demands.
examples: The castle was besieged by enemy soldiers for three long months.
The celebrity was besieged by fans the moment she stepped outside.
After the announcement, the helpline was besieged with calls from worried parents.
The small town was besieged by reporters following the dramatic rescue.
He felt besieged by homework from every subject at the same time.

entries.meaning: The process of filling or sealing seams and gaps to make them watertight or airtight.
examples: The builder used caulking to seal the gap around the bathtub.
She applied fresh caulking around the window frames to keep the cold air out.
The boat needed caulking along its hull before it could safely go to sea.
A tube of caulking is an essential item for any home repair kit.
The caulking around the shower had worn away and needed to be replaced.

entries.meaning: Mercy and leniency shown towards someone; the quality of being kind and forgiving.
examples: The judge showed clemency and gave the young offender a lighter sentence.
She begged for clemency on behalf of her brother, explaining his difficult circumstances.
The king was known for his clemency towards defeated enemies who surrendered peacefully.
Showing clemency does not mean ignoring wrongdoing — it means responding with compassion.
The crowd pleaded for clemency as the verdict was read out in the courtroom.

entries.meaning: To force or oblige someone to do something; to drive someone to act.
examples: The new law compels all passengers to wear a seatbelt in the back seat.
She felt compelled to speak up when she saw something was wrong.
The evidence was so strong that it compelled the jury to reach a verdict quickly.
Nothing could compel him to change his mind once it was made up.
A sense of duty compelled her to stay behind and help clear up after the event.

entries.meaning: Not openly acknowledged or displayed; done in a hidden or secretive way.
examples: The spy carried out a covert operation to gather information without being detected.
She sent a covert message to her friend during the dull assembly.
The police launched a covert investigation into the suspicious activity.
He gave her a covert glance from across the room, trying not to be noticed.
The team used covert cameras to monitor the wildlife without disturbing the animals.

entries.meaning: In a state of disrepair through age, neglect, or wear; run-down.
examples: The dilapidated farmhouse had broken windows and a crumbling roof.
They bought a dilapidated cottage and spent years restoring it to its former glory.
The children dared each other to explore the dilapidated building at the edge of town.
The garden wall had become so dilapidated that it collapsed in the storm.
A dilapidated old bicycle leaned against the fence, its tyres completely flat.

entries.meaning: A house, flat, or other place where a person lives; a place of residence.
examples: The archaeologists uncovered the remains of an ancient dwelling near the river.
