Every dwelling in the street had been decorated with lights for the festival.
The family's dwelling was small but cosy and filled with warmth.
A cave was the earliest form of human dwelling before houses were built.
Planning permission is required before converting a barn into a dwelling.

entries.meaning: Done with excessive speed or urgency; acting too quickly without care.
examples: She made a hasty decision that she later deeply regretted.
In his hasty rush to leave, he forgot to take his packed lunch.
A hasty reply can often cause more problems than a thoughtful one.
The hasty repairs to the roof did not last through the winter storms.
He was warned not to make any hasty judgements before hearing both sides.

entries.meaning: Unable to be touched or grasped physically; difficult to define or measure precisely.
examples: Love and loyalty are intangible qualities that cannot be measured or weighed.
The painting had an intangible quality that made it impossible to look away.
The value of kindness is intangible but its effects are felt deeply.
She sensed an intangible change in the atmosphere as soon as she walked in.
Trust is an intangible bond that takes years to build but moments to break.

entries.meaning: An event or sign believed to foretell a future occurrence, either good or evil.
examples: The black cloud gathering on the horizon felt like an omen of bad weather ahead.
Many cultures consider a rainbow to be a good omen after a storm.
She took finding a four-leaf clover as a lucky omen for her exam.
The sudden silence of the birds was considered an omen of danger in the old story.
He dismissed the broken mirror as a silly superstition rather than an evil omen.

entries.meaning: A feather, especially a long ornamental one; a long spreading cloud of smoke, dust, or water.
examples: The knight wore a magnificent plume of white feathers on his helmet.
A plume of dark smoke rose from the chimney of the old factory.
The peacock fanned out its spectacular plume to attract a mate.
A plume of steam shot upwards as the train pulled into the station.
She decorated her hat with a single elegant plume for the formal occasion.

entries.meaning: Affectedly grand, solemn, or self-important in manner or speech.
examples: The pompous mayor insisted on giving a long speech at every public event.
His pompous attitude made it difficult for others to approach him with questions.
She found his pompous tone irritating, especially when he was often wrong.
The pompous professor spoke as though he were the only expert in the room.
He gave a pompous wave of his hand as if dismissing everything she had said.

entries.meaning: Attractively unusual or old-fashioned in a charming or endearing way.
examples: They stayed in a quaint little cottage with a thatched roof and climbing roses.
The village was full of quaint cobbled streets and ancient stone buildings.
She found the old customs of the island quaint but rather fascinating.
The shop had a quaint wooden sign hanging above the door.
He sent a quaint handwritten letter instead of an email, which she found charming.

entries.meaning: To live in or at a particular place; to be situated or based somewhere.
examples: The family has resided in the same village for over three generations.
The power to make decisions resides with the head of the organisation.
She currently resides in Edinburgh but was born in Cardiff.
Several rare species of bird reside in the nature reserve all year round.
The ambassador resides in a grand official building near the parliament.

entries.meaning: Strict, severe, and uncompromising in manner or attitude.
examples: The stern headteacher insisted on absolute silence during assembly.
Her father gave her a stern look that told her the conversation was over.
The coach was stern about punctuality — lateness was simply not tolerated.
Despite his stern appearance, the teacher was caring and fair.
A stern warning from the referee was enough to calm the players down.

entries.meaning: Quiet and rather reflective or low in spirits; less intense than usual.
examples: The team were subdued after losing the match in the final minute.
She spoke in a subdued tone, clearly upset by the news she had received.
The lighting in the restaurant was soft and subdued, creating a calm atmosphere.
After the argument, the house felt strangely subdued and silent.
He was uncharacteristically subdued at the party, barely saying a word all evening.

entries.meaning: To become dry and shrivelled; to lose or cause to lose vitality and freshness.
examples: The flowers began to wither after three days without water.
His confidence started to wither under the pressure of the exam.
The drought caused the crops to wither in the fields before harvest.
She watched sadly as the last rose in the vase began to wither.
Without encouragement, even the greatest talent can wither and fade.

entries.meaning: to combine resources for a mutual benefit; a partner or friend who supports you.
examples: The two small countries decided to ally with each other against the larger nation.
In times of difficulty, it helps to have a trusted ally by your side.
The school decided to ally itself with a local charity to raise money for good causes.
An ally is someone who supports and helps you, especially in a difficult situation.
The hero and the wizard became allies to defeat the evil dragon.

entries.meaning: hostile and aggressive; eager to argue or fight.
examples: The belligerent man picked a fight with everyone he met at the market.
His belligerent tone made the conversation very difficult.
The two belligerent nations could not agree on a peace treaty.
The belligerent dog barked and growled at anyone who came near the gate.
Try not to be belligerent; a calm approach is usually more effective.

entries.meaning: openly declared or admitted; asserting something publicly.
examples: He is an avowed supporter of the local football team and makes no secret of it.
She is an avowed vegetarian who has not eaten meat for ten years.
The politician made an avowed commitment to reduce taxes if elected.
His avowed intention was to become a doctor, and he worked hard towards that goal.
The avowed aim of the charity is to provide clean water for all.

entries.meaning: burnt and blackened by fire or heat.
examples: The charred remains of the bonfire were still visible in the garden.
The firefighters found only charred wood where the old barn had once stood.
She accidentally left the toast too long and it came out completely charred.
The charred edges of the old map showed that it had survived a fire.
All that remained after the blaze was a pile of charred timber and ash.

entries.meaning: to persistently and gently persuade someone to do something.
examples: She managed to coax the frightened kitten out from under the bed.
He had to coax his little sister into trying the new food.
The trainer coaxed the horse gently over the high jump.
No amount of coaxing could persuade him to change his mind.
She coaxed a smile out of the shy child with a funny face.

entries.meaning: living or occurring at the same time; modern and present-day.
examples: Shakespeare and Marlowe were contemporary writers who both worked in Elizabethan England.
The museum has a large collection of contemporary art by living artists.
She prefers contemporary music to classical pieces.
A contemporary of Einstein, Marie Curie was also a brilliant scientist.
The building was designed in a contemporary style with glass and steel.

entries.meaning: excessively proud of oneself; having an inflated opinion of one's own abilities.
examples: He was so conceited that he spent more time admiring himself than helping others.
The conceited footballer boasted about his skills to anyone who would listen.
She found his conceited attitude very off-putting.
A conceited person believes they are better than everyone else.
Despite her great talent, she was never conceited or boastful.

entries.meaning: based on or in accordance with what is generally accepted or done; traditional.
examples: The family lived in a conventional house with a garden and a car on the drive.
He chose a conventional career in law rather than pursuing his dream of painting.
Conventional wisdom says that you should always save a little money each month.
She rejected the conventional way of doing things and invented her own method.
The scientist challenged conventional thinking with his groundbreaking new theory.

entries.meaning: a loud, unpleasant, and prolonged noise; a continuous uproar.
examples: The din from the construction site made it impossible to concentrate.
The children's playground was full of the din of shouting and laughter.
She had to raise her voice to be heard above the din of the crowd.
The factory produced an unpleasant din that could be heard from the street.
After the concert, the din of the instruments slowly faded into silence.

entries.meaning: to escape from or avoid something in a clever or cunning way; to be difficult to find or remember.
examples: The cunning fox managed to elude the hunters for several hours.
The answer to the puzzle continued to elude him, no matter how hard he thought.
The suspect eluded the police by disguising himself and slipping through the back door.
Fame had always eluded him, despite his many years of hard work.
The rare butterfly seemed to elude every attempt to photograph it.

entries.meaning: causing a mood of gloom or depression; bleak and dreary.
examples: The dismal weather made everyone feel miserable and gloomy.
The team put in a dismal performance and lost by six goals.
The abandoned house looked dismal and unwelcoming in the grey light.
She felt dismal after receiving the disappointing exam results.
The winter months can be dismal, with short days and little sunlight.

entries.meaning: a spiral shape; a three-dimensional curve that winds around like a spring or corkscrew.
examples: DNA is shaped like a double helix, which looks like a twisted ladder.
The staircase wound upwards in a graceful helix.
The spring inside the pen is made in the shape of a helix.
In science class, we learned that a helix is a special type of spiral shape.
The shell of the snail forms a perfect helix as it grows.

entries.meaning: not showing due respect; boldly rude and disrespectful.
examples: The impudent boy answered back to the teacher and was sent out of the class.
It was impudent of him to interrupt the headteacher in the middle of her speech.
She gave an impudent grin and refused to apologise.
His impudent remarks upset many of the older guests at the dinner.
An impudent child often ends up in trouble for their lack of respect.

entries.meaning: fond of company; sociable and enjoying the company of others.
examples: She is a gregarious person who loves being around people and going to parties.
Lions are gregarious animals that live and hunt in groups called prides.
His gregarious nature made him popular with everyone he met.
A gregarious person finds it easy to make new friends in any situation.
He was so gregarious that he never liked spending time alone.

entries.meaning: marking the beginning of an institution, activity, or period of office; first.
examples: The president gave a powerful speech at his inaugural ceremony.
It was the inaugural meeting of the new science club at school.
The singer performed at the inaugural concert of the new theatre.
This year marks the inaugural edition of the international book festival.
The team played their inaugural match in front of a packed home crowd.

entries.meaning: to express grief or sorrow; a passionate expression of sadness or mourning.
examples: The villagers gathered to lament the loss of their beloved leader.
She could hear the lament of the bagpipes drifting across the hills.
He lamented the fact that so many old buildings had been knocked down.
A lament is a song or poem that expresses deep grief or sadness.
There was no time to lament their defeat; they had to prepare for the next match.

entries.meaning: to suffer complete ruin or destruction; to die, especially in a sudden way.
examples: Many ancient civilisations perished due to drought, war, or disease.
The plants will perish if they are not watered regularly.
Sailors used to perish at sea when storms destroyed their ships.
Perish the thought of failing your exams after all that hard work!
Without sunlight, most living things would quickly perish.

entries.meaning: to fail to resist pressure, temptation, or illness; to give way.
examples: She tried to resist the chocolate cake but eventually succumbed to temptation.
The brave defender refused to succumb to the pressure of the opposing team.
He succumbed to his illness after a long battle and passed away peacefully.
Many people succumb to stress when they have too much work to do.
It is important not to succumb to peer pressure and to make your own choices.

entries.meaning: characterized by pretentious or showy display designed to impress others.
examples: The billionaire lived in an ostentatious mansion filled with gold furniture.
She found his ostentatious jewellery and expensive clothes rather vulgar.
The ostentatious parade was designed to show off the country's military power.
He drove an ostentatious sports car just to get people's attention.
An ostentatious person wants everyone to notice how rich or important they are.

entries.meaning: deceit used in order to achieve one's goal; a trick or scheme used to hide the truth.
examples: He used subterfuge to sneak into the building without anyone noticing.
The spy relied on subterfuge and disguise to gather information.
It was discovered that the company had been using subterfuge to hide its losses.
Subterfuge is the use of clever tricks to deceive others.
She resorted to subterfuge to avoid telling her parents where she had really been.

entries.meaning: following a winding course; (of a river or road) curving and twisting rather than going in a straight line.
examples: The meandering river snaked lazily through the green valley.
We took a meandering path through the woods to reach the cottage.
Her meandering speech wandered from one topic to another without ever reaching a point.
The meandering country lane was lined with wildflowers and old stone walls.
After lunch, we went on a meandering walk along the riverbank.

entries.meaning: having a lot of space inside; roomy and able to hold a great deal.
examples: She carried a capacious handbag that held everything from books to an umbrella.
The capacious hall could easily seat over a thousand guests.
Their new house had a capacious kitchen with plenty of room for cooking together.
A capacious boot is essential for a family car going on long holidays.
The library's capacious reading room was filled with sunlight and tall shelves.

entries.meaning: to pour a liquid gradually from one container into another, especially without disturbing the sediment.
examples: He carefully decanted the wine into a glass jug before the meal.
She decanted the soup from the pot into a serving bowl.
To decant a liquid means to pour it slowly so that any sediment is left behind.
The chemist decanted the clear solution into a smaller flask.
They decanted the olive oil into a pretty bottle for the dinner table.

entries.meaning: to long for something, especially something belonging to someone else.
examples: He had always coveted his neighbour's bright red sports car.
The young pianist coveted the prize awarded to the best musician each year.
To covet something means to want it badly, often when it isn't yours to have.
She tried not to covet her friend's new bicycle, but it was hard not to admire it.
Many athletes covet an Olympic gold medal above any other prize.

entries.meaning: serious and immediate danger; the risk of being harmed or destroyed.
examples: The sailors were in great peril as the storm crashed against their ship.
Climbing the cliff at night put the explorers in serious peril.
She warned us of the perils of crossing the busy road without looking.
Peril is a word used to describe a situation of extreme danger.
The hero rescued the children from the peril of the burning building.

entries.meaning: considered holy and deserving great respect; very important and not to be changed or harmed.
examples: The temple was a sacred place where worshippers came to pray in silence.
To many people, family traditions are sacred and must be carefully preserved.
The ancient text was treated as a sacred object and kept in a glass case.
A sacred site is one that is considered holy by a particular religion or culture.
He believed that his promise to his grandfather was sacred and could never be broken.

entries.meaning: to send someone away, especially from a job; to refuse to consider an idea seriously.
examples: The teacher dismissed the class as soon as the bell rang.
The manager had to dismiss the employee for repeatedly arriving late.
He dismissed her suggestion without even thinking about it properly.
Don't dismiss the idea too quickly; it might turn out to be useful.
The judge dismissed the case because there was not enough evidence.

entries.meaning: to grow or develop in a healthy or vigorous way; (n) a bold or extravagant gesture or action.
examples: Roses flourish in soil that is rich and well-drained.
The small business began to flourish after it opened a website.
Her artistic talent flourished once she joined the painting club.
He signed his name with a great flourish at the bottom of the letter.
To flourish means to grow strongly or to be very successful.

entries.meaning: a holy place where people worship or remember a sacred person or event.
examples: Pilgrims travelled for many days to visit the shrine high in the mountains.
A small shrine stood at the side of the road, decorated with flowers.
The room had been turned into a shrine to her favourite singer, with posters everywhere.
A shrine is a special place dedicated to a god, saint, or important memory.
They lit candles at the shrine to remember loved ones who had passed away.

entries.meaning: showing no interest or concern about something or someone.
examples: He seemed completely indifferent to whether his team won or lost.
The cat was indifferent to the new toy we had bought for it.
She gave an indifferent shrug when asked which film she wanted to watch.
To be indifferent means not to care one way or the other about something.
The audience grew indifferent as the long, dull speech continued.

entries.meaning: a disease or illness; a serious problem or unhealthy condition.
examples: The doctor was unable to identify the strange malady that had struck the village.
Loneliness is a malady that affects many people in big cities.
Coughing and sneezing are common symptoms of this winter malady.
A malady is another word for an illness, especially one that lasts a long time.
The old gardener suffered from a mysterious malady that left him very tired.

entries.meaning: to decide or settle something firmly; to discover the facts about something.
examples: The judges will determine the winner of the competition tomorrow.
Scientists tried to determine the cause of the unusual weather.
She was determined to finish the marathon, no matter how tired she felt.
To determine something means to make a firm decision or to find it out.
The detective worked carefully to determine who had taken the missing necklace.

entries.meaning: intelligently analytical and clear-thinking; expressing an idea sharply and accurately.
examples: The journalist was famous for her incisive questions during interviews.
He gave an incisive analysis of the football match in just a few sentences.
Her incisive comments quickly got to the heart of the problem.
An incisive mind can cut straight through confusing information to find the truth.
The teacher praised the pupil's incisive answer for being both short and exact.

entries.meaning: to officially declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.
examples: New evidence was found that completely exonerated the accused man.
The investigation exonerated the teacher of any blame for the accident.
To exonerate someone is to prove that they did not do something wrong.
The court exonerated her after the real culprit confessed.
The report exonerated the company of any responsibility for the leak.

entries.meaning: widespread; existing or happening often or in many places.
examples: Coughs and colds are particularly prevalent during the winter months.
The use of mobile phones is now prevalent among children of all ages.
Old-fashioned customs are still prevalent in some parts of the countryside.
If something is prevalent, it is found very commonly in a place or group.
Smartwatches have become increasingly prevalent over the past few years.

entries.meaning: very careful and thorough about details; behaving in a strictly honest way.
examples: The scientist kept scrupulous notes of every experiment she carried out.
He was scrupulous about returning every coin he had borrowed.
The hotel was scrupulous in its cleanliness, with not a speck of dust anywhere.
A scrupulous person pays great attention to detail and behaves very honestly.
She was scrupulous in following the recipe exactly as it was written.

entries.meaning: extremely happy and excited, especially because something good has happened.
examples: She was elated when she heard she had been chosen for the team.
The whole family felt elated after their long-awaited holiday was finally booked.
He looked elated as he held up his shiny gold trophy.
To be elated means to feel a wonderful, soaring sense of happiness.
The elated crowd cheered loudly as the winning goal was scored.

entries.meaning: to make something larger, greater, or stronger by adding to it.
examples: He took a weekend job to augment his pocket money.
The orchestra augmented its sound by adding extra strings for the concert.
She read widely to augment her knowledge before the exam.
To augment something is to add to it so that it becomes bigger or better.
The company hired more staff to augment its small design team.

entries.meaning: to invent or make up something false in order to deceive; to construct or manufacture an object.
examples: He tried to fabricate an excuse for missing his homework, but no one believed him.
The witness was caught having fabricated her story about the accident.
The factory fabricates parts for cars and aeroplanes.
To fabricate means either to make something or to invent a false story.
She fabricated a clever model of a castle out of cardboard and tape.

entries.meaning: relating to one's home, family, or country, rather than to other countries; (of animals) kept by humans.
examples: She enjoyed quiet domestic life with her family on the weekends.
The shop sells a range of domestic appliances, from kettles to washing machines.
Domestic flights take off and land within the same country.
Cats and dogs are popular domestic animals in many homes.
The country tries to support its own domestic industries before relying on imports.

entries.meaning: (of a bad action) very obvious and shocking; openly done without any attempt to hide it.
examples: He was sent off for a flagrant foul during the football match.
The flagrant lie was so obvious that no one was fooled by it.
Cheating in plain sight of the teacher was a flagrant act of dishonesty.
A flagrant breach of the rules will result in immediate disqualification.
She showed a flagrant disregard for the school uniform policy.

entries.meaning: producing a great number or amount of something; very fruitful or productive.
examples: The author was prolific, writing more than fifty novels in her lifetime.
Rabbits are well known for being prolific breeders.
The apple tree was so prolific that we had baskets of fruit to give away.
He was a prolific goal-scorer, finding the net almost every game.
A prolific writer is one who produces a great deal of work.

entries.meaning: the quality of being the same as or very similar to others; lack of variety.
examples: The school insisted on uniformity in its pupils' appearance and behaviour.
There was a pleasing uniformity in the rows of newly painted houses.
Some uniformity in the shop signs gave the high street a tidy look.
Uniformity means that things are all the same or follow a strict pattern.
He complained that the uniformity of the food at school made every lunch feel the same.

entries.meaning: to make secret or new information known; to reveal something hidden.
examples: The company refused to disclose how much money it had lost.
She finally disclosed the secret she had kept for many years.
The doctor cannot disclose details about a patient without permission.
To disclose something is to share information that was previously hidden.
He disclosed that he had been working on a surprise gift for his mother.

entries.meaning: (v) to make use of someone or something unfairly for one's own advantage; (n) a brave or notable deed.
examples: The factory was accused of exploiting its workers by paying very low wages.
He tried to exploit his friend's kindness by always borrowing money.
Companies often exploit new technology to make their products better.
The book described the daring exploits of the famous explorer.
To exploit someone is to use them unfairly for your own benefit.

entries.meaning: following a fixed pattern or set of rules; predictable and lacking originality.
examples: The film was criticised for being too formulaic and lacking surprises.
Pop songs sometimes have a formulaic structure of verse, chorus, verse.
Her formulaic answers showed she had memorised them from a textbook.
Something formulaic follows a tried-and-tested pattern that rarely changes.
The teacher encouraged the class to avoid formulaic openings in their stories.

entries.meaning: the complete loss or absence of hope; (v) to lose all hope.
examples: After the third defeat in a row, the team sank into despair.
He stared at the broken vase in despair, knowing it had been his grandmother's favourite.
Don't despair; you can always try the test again next term.
Despair is a feeling of having no hope left at all.
She refused to despair, even when things looked very difficult.

entries.meaning: to draw out or bring forth a response, fact, or reaction from someone.
examples: The teacher's funny joke elicited a burst of laughter from the class.
The lawyer asked careful questions to elicit the truth from the witness.
Her sad story elicited sympathy from everyone in the room.
To elicit something means to bring it out, often a reaction or piece of information.
The advert was designed to elicit a strong emotional response from viewers.

entries.meaning: intending to do harm or cause hurt to others; spiteful.
examples: The malicious gossip spread quickly and hurt many feelings.
He sent a malicious email designed to upset his classmate.
There was a malicious smile on the villain's face as he watched the trap close.
Computers can be infected by malicious software that damages files.
Something malicious is meant to cause harm or pain to someone else.

entries.meaning: arranged in a tidy and orderly way; (of a drink) not diluted with water or other liquid.
examples: Her bedroom was always neat, with every book in its proper place.
He prefers his apple juice neat, without any extra water.
The neat rows of vegetables in the garden looked beautiful.
His handwriting was so neat that it almost looked printed.
Try to keep your desk neat so you can find what you need.

entries.meaning: allowing light to pass through so that objects behind can be clearly seen; open, honest, and easy to understand.
examples: The transparent glass walls let sunlight stream into every room.
The teacher's instructions were transparent and easy to follow.
The school promised to be transparent about how the money was spent.
Something transparent can either be see-through or completely honest.
The water was so transparent you could see the pebbles at the bottom of the stream.

entries.meaning: closely connected by friendship or affection; small and warmly cosy.
examples: They had an intimate chat by the fire late into the evening.
The little café had an intimate atmosphere with soft music and candles.
Only her most intimate friends knew about her plan to surprise everyone.
An intimate gathering is a small, friendly meeting between people who know each other well.
The two sisters shared an intimate bond that no one else could match.

entries.meaning: not active or growing for a period of time, but able to become active again.
examples: The volcano had been dormant for hundreds of years before erupting again.
Bears remain dormant for much of the winter while they hibernate.
Many seeds lie dormant under the soil until the spring rains arrive.
Her interest in painting had been dormant since she was young.
Something dormant is resting but ready to become active again.

entries.meaning: average in amount, intensity, or degree, not extreme; (v) to make less extreme.
examples: There was a moderate amount of traffic on the road this morning.
He runs at a moderate pace so he doesn't get too tired.
The teacher tried to moderate the heated debate between the two pupils.
A moderate climate is neither very hot nor very cold.
Try to be moderate when eating sweets; too many can make you ill.

entries.meaning: enough for a particular purpose or need.
examples: There was sufficient food at the party for everyone to have seconds.
We had just sufficient time to catch the train before it left.
The blanket was not sufficient to keep him warm during the cold night.
Sufficient means enough — not too much and not too little.
Make sure you have sufficient water with you on a long walk.

entries.meaning: an opinion or guess based on incomplete information; (v) to form such an opinion.
examples: Without evidence, his theory was nothing more than conjecture.
The detective refused to make any conjecture before she had the facts.
There has been much conjecture about the cause of the strange noise.
Conjecture means making a guess without having proper proof.
We can only conjecture about what really happened that stormy night.

entries.meaning: to give someone a job; to make use of something.
examples: The factory employs over two hundred people from the local town.
She decided to employ a clever trick to solve the puzzle.
The company employed new staff to help with the busy holiday season.
To employ someone is to hire them to do a job for you.
He employed a calm voice to settle the noisy children.

entries.meaning: floating without being moored or steered; without purpose or direction.
examples: The little boat was set adrift on the calm blue sea.
After leaving school, he felt adrift and unsure what to do next.
The rope snapped, and the raft drifted adrift down the river.
To be adrift is to float along, or to feel lost without direction.
The young puppy seemed adrift in the huge new garden.

entries.meaning: to express strong disapproval of someone or something; to sentence to a punishment.
examples: World leaders condemned the cruel attack on the helpless village.
The judge condemned the criminal to a long stay in prison.
She condemned bullying in any form during her assembly speech.
To condemn someone is to strongly disapprove of what they have done.
The old building was condemned because it was no longer safe.

entries.meaning: relating to or situated on the edge or outer boundary; of secondary importance.
examples: He could see something move at the peripheral edge of his vision.
The discussion focused on the main problem, leaving peripheral issues for later.
A keyboard and mouse are common peripheral devices used with a computer.
Something peripheral is on the edge or is of less importance.
The peripheral roads around the city are usually less busy than the centre.

entries.meaning: the great size, extent, or importance of something.
examples: The magnitude of the earthquake shocked scientists around the world.
We did not at first realise the magnitude of the problem.
Stars are classified by their magnitude, or how bright they appear in the sky.
The magnitude of his kindness was clear to everyone he helped.
Magnitude is a word that describes the size or importance of something.

entries.meaning: to make someone firmly believe that something is true or right.
examples: She tried to convince her parents to let her have a pet rabbit.
The lawyer convinced the jury that her client was innocent.
He convinced himself that everything would turn out fine in the end.
To convince someone is to make them believe what you are saying.
The salesperson failed to convince me that I needed a new phone.

entries.meaning: to escape from or avoid being caught, often by being clever.
examples: The clever fox managed to elude the hunters once again.
The answer to the riddle continued to elude her all afternoon.
The thief eluded the police by hiding inside an empty barn.
Sleep eluded him as he lay awake worrying about the test.
To elude someone is to escape from them in a clever way.

entries.meaning: of, from, or like God or a god; extremely good or delightful.
examples: In many stories, kings were said to rule by divine right.
The chocolate cake tasted absolutely divine.
Ancient peoples believed that thunder was a sign of divine anger.
The painting showed a divine figure surrounded by golden light.
Something divine is connected to a god or is wonderfully good.

entries.meaning: to place, fit, or push something into something else.
examples: Please insert the key into the lock and turn it gently.
She inserted a new battery into the remote control.
The teacher asked him to insert a comma in the correct place.
To insert something is to put it inside or between other things.
He inserted a bookmark to keep his place in the long novel.

entries.meaning: to formally accuse or charge someone with a serious crime.
examples: The court decided to indict the man on charges of theft.
To indict someone means to officially say they have committed a crime.
The grand jury chose to indict the company for breaking safety rules.
He was indicted for fraud after a long police investigation.
The newspaper article seemed to indict the entire system as unfair.

entries.meaning: not attracting attention; hard to see or notice.
examples: He chose an inconspicuous seat at the back of the room.
The little bird's brown feathers made it inconspicuous against the bark.
She wore inconspicuous clothes so that no one would recognise her.
Something inconspicuous blends in and is not easily seen.
The tiny door was inconspicuous, hidden behind a tall bookshelf.

entries.meaning: pretending to be shy or modest, especially as a way of attracting attention.
examples: She gave a coy smile when asked who her secret friend was.
He was coy about his birthday plans, refusing to share any details.
The actress was coy in interviews about her new film role.
Someone who is coy pretends to be shyer than they really are.
Don't be coy — tell us what you really think of the new design.

entries.meaning: an item of clothing.
examples: The shop sold beautiful garments made from soft Indian silk.
She carefully folded each garment and placed it in the suitcase.
The royal garment was decorated with gold thread and tiny jewels.
A garment is simply a piece of clothing that someone wears.
The tailor mended the torn garment so that it looked brand new.

entries.meaning: producing no useful result; pointless and likely to fail.
examples: It was futile to argue with him once he had made up his mind.
Their attempts to reach the summit before nightfall proved futile.
Trying to empty the flooded basement with a small bucket felt futile.
Something futile is a waste of time because it cannot succeed.
She made one last, futile effort to find her lost ring in the sand.

entries.meaning: free from pretence or deceit; genuine in feelings, thoughts, or actions.
examples: She gave a sincere apology for the hurtful thing she had said.
His thanks were sincere, and you could see he really meant them.
A sincere friend will always tell you the truth, even when it is hard.
To be sincere means to truly mean what you say or do.
He wrote a sincere letter to his grandmother to thank her for the gift.

entries.meaning: a statement or theory put forward as a premise to be proved; a long piece of academic writing on a particular subject.
examples: Her thesis was that early reading helps children to do better at school.
He spent two years writing his thesis on the history of the local railway.
The teacher asked us to state our thesis clearly at the start of the essay.
A thesis is a long piece of writing that argues for a particular idea.
Every paragraph of the report supported her main thesis.

entries.meaning: to make a serious, formal promise; (n) such a promise.
examples: The mayor pledged to build a new park for the children of the town.
They took a pledge of friendship that would last all their lives.
She pledged to give half her pocket money to charity each week.
To pledge something is to promise it solemnly and seriously.
The class made a pledge to keep their classroom tidy every day.

entries.meaning: a very slight difference in meaning, feeling, sound, or colour.
examples: There is a fine nuance between feeling sad and feeling disappointed.
The painter captured every nuance of light on the calm lake.
He missed the nuance in her voice that hinted she was annoyed.
A nuance is a small difference that is easy to overlook.
Good actors understand the nuances of every character they play.

entries.meaning: in accordance with the highest standards; without flaw or fault.
examples: The waiter offered impeccable service throughout the long meal.
Her manners were impeccable; she always remembered to say thank you.
He wore an impeccable white suit to the wedding.
Something impeccable is so well done that nothing about it can be criticised.
The pianist's impeccable performance was rewarded with a standing ovation.

entries.meaning: a person who betrays a friend, country, cause, or trust.
examples: The soldier was branded a traitor for selling secrets to the enemy.
To call someone a traitor is to say they have betrayed those who trusted them.
The story tells of a traitor who let invaders into the castle at night.
Friends never expected him to turn out to be a traitor.
History remembers many traitors whose treachery changed the course of nations.

entries.meaning: completely confused and unable to understand what is happening.
examples: The bewildered tourist stood in the busy square trying to read his map.
She gave a bewildered look when asked the difficult maths question.
The puppy was bewildered by all the noise in the busy market.
A bewildered person feels lost and unable to make sense of things.
He was completely bewildered by the strange machine on the table.

entries.meaning: nearness in space, time, or relationship.
examples: The hotel's proximity to the beach made it very popular with families.
Because of the proximity of the holidays, the shops were extremely busy.
She felt safer when she was in close proximity to her parents.
Proximity is a fancy way of saying how near something is.
The library's proximity to my house means I can pop in every week.

entries.meaning: a person who is among the first to explore or develop a new area, idea, or method.
examples: She was a pioneer of women's rights in the early twentieth century.
The pioneers travelled west in covered wagons to start new lives.
The scientist pioneered a new way of treating the disease.
A pioneer is someone who is first to do something important.
The company pioneered the use of electric cars in our country.

entries.meaning: behaving in a way that contradicts what one claims to believe or feel.
examples: It was hypocritical of him to scold others for being late when he was always late himself.
She found his speech about kindness rather hypocritical given his cruel actions.
People dislike hypocritical leaders who don't follow their own rules.
To be hypocritical is to say one thing while doing the opposite.
The class agreed it would be hypocritical to demand respect without giving it.

entries.meaning: done according to a careful, systematic, and orderly plan.
examples: The detective took a methodical approach, examining every clue carefully.
She was methodical in her revision, making notes for each topic in turn.
The scientist's methodical work led to an important discovery.
Being methodical means working in a careful, ordered way.
He cleaned his room in a methodical fashion, starting in one corner and working around.

entries.meaning: of extreme force, strength, or feeling.
examples: The intense heat of the desert made walking very difficult.
She felt an intense sadness when her old dog finally passed away.
There was an intense look on his face as he tried to solve the puzzle.
The colours of the sunset were intense and breathtakingly beautiful.
Something intense is felt or experienced very strongly.

entries.meaning: a small part broken off or separated from something; (v) to break into small pieces.
examples: She picked up a fragment of the broken vase from the kitchen floor.
Only a fragment of the ancient scroll has survived to this day.
He could remember just a fragment of the dream after he woke up.
The glass fragmented into hundreds of tiny pieces when it hit the ground.
A fragment is a small part of something larger that has been broken or separated.

entries.meaning: to obtain something, especially with care or effort.
examples: After much searching, she managed to procure tickets for the sold-out concert.
The chef was determined to procure only the freshest ingredients.
He procured a rare old book from a tiny shop in the back streets.
To procure something is to obtain it, often after some effort.
The school procured new computers for the library after a long fundraising drive.

entries.meaning: to give up something valuable for the sake of something else; (n) the act of giving something up.
examples: She sacrificed her weekend in order to finish the school project on time.
Their parents made many sacrifices to send them to a good school.
The footballer sacrificed an easy goal so that his teammate could score.
To sacrifice something is to give it up for the sake of something more important.
The brave knight made the ultimate sacrifice to save the kingdom.

entries.meaning: to put something upside down or in the opposite position, order, or arrangement.
examples: He inverted the bottle so that the last drop of sauce would come out.
To make the cake easier to remove, invert the tin onto a wire rack.
The photographer inverted the colours of the picture for an unusual effect.
To invert means to turn something upside down or back to front.
She inverted the order of her notes and the story made much more sense.

entries.meaning: attractively unusual or old-fashioned.
examples: We stayed in a quaint little cottage with a thatched roof.
The quaint old village seemed unchanged for hundreds of years.
She wore a quaint hat decorated with silk flowers and ribbons.
Something quaint is charming because it is old-fashioned or unusual.
The bookshop had a quaint sign hanging above its narrow wooden door.

entries.meaning: acting with or showing care and thought for the future; sensible.
examples: It is prudent to save some of your pocket money for emergencies.
The prudent driver slowed down as the road became icy.
She made a prudent decision to take an umbrella, even though the sky was clear.
A prudent person thinks carefully before acting.
It would be prudent to revise a little every day rather than panic the night before.

entries.meaning: (v) to hold someone closely in one's arms; to accept an idea willingly; (n) a hug.
examples: She ran to embrace her brother after his long journey home.
The school decided to embrace new technology in the classroom.
Many people embrace healthy habits as they grow older.
To embrace something can mean to hug it or to accept it warmly.
He gave his grandmother a gentle embrace before leaving.

entries.meaning: (v) to put a decision or plan into effect; (n) a tool or instrument used for a job.
examples: The school plans to implement a new homework policy next term.
The gardener used a sharp implement to dig up the weeds.
They worked hard to implement the changes the teacher had suggested.
To implement a plan means to actually carry it out.
A spade is a useful implement for gardening.

entries.meaning: to delay or prevent something by getting in the way.
examples: The fallen tree impeded traffic along the country lane.
Loud noise can impede a child's ability to concentrate on schoolwork.
Heavy boots impeded his progress through the deep snow.
To impede something is to slow it down or get in its way.
Nothing could impede her determination to win the gold medal.

entries.meaning: out of place; not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or other things.
examples: A modern glass tower looked incongruous among the old stone cottages.
His cheerful song seemed incongruous in the quiet, sad room.
The bright pink chair was incongruous with the rest of the simple grey furniture.
Something incongruous looks strange or wrong in its setting.
It felt incongruous to wear shorts in the middle of a snowstorm.

entries.meaning: the highest point of a mountain or hill; a meeting between heads of government.
examples: After many hours of climbing, they finally reached the summit of the mountain.
World leaders met at the climate summit to discuss the environment.
From the summit, we could see for miles across the green valleys.
A summit is the very top of something, or a very important meeting.
The flag was planted proudly at the summit by the brave team of climbers.

entries.meaning: to make something clear by explaining it; to throw light on a subject.
examples: The teacher elucidated the difficult problem with a simple drawing.
Could you elucidate exactly what you mean by that statement?
The author elucidated her ideas in the introduction to the book.
To elucidate something is to make it clear and easier to understand.
The guide elucidated the meaning of the ancient symbols on the wall.

entries.meaning: comically or repulsively ugly or distorted; strange and unpleasant.
examples: Stone gargoyles with grotesque faces lined the roof of the old church.
The story described a grotesque creature lurking in the dark forest.
He pulled a grotesque face that made the younger children giggle.
Something grotesque is very strange and ugly in an unsettling way.
The mask was so grotesque that no one wanted to wear it for the play.

entries.meaning: (v) to indicate one is not willing to do something; (n, refuse) waste material or rubbish.
examples: He refused to leave the playground until his friend had arrived.
She politely refused a second helping of pudding.
The dog refused to come inside, no matter how loudly we called.
The lorry collected the household refuse from each driveway.
To refuse something is to say no to it firmly.

entries.meaning: fluent, persuasive, and clear in speaking or writing.
examples: The head teacher gave an eloquent speech about kindness at the assembly.
Her eloquent letter convinced the council to save the local park.
He was eloquent in defending his point of view during the debate.
An eloquent speaker is one who can express ideas clearly and powerfully.
The poem was a short but eloquent tribute to the brave firefighters.

entries.meaning: (n) something bought for less than its usual price; (v) to negotiate the price.
examples: The shoes were a real bargain in the end-of-summer sale.
She bargained with the market trader and got a lower price for the basket.
At only one pound, the second-hand book was an absolute bargain.
To strike a bargain means to come to an agreement that suits both sides.
A bargain is something you buy at a much lower price than usual.

entries.meaning: to put an end to something, especially by force; to calm strong feelings.
examples: The teacher quickly quelled the noisy argument at the back of the class.
A few kind words from her mother helped to quell her fears about the test.
The soldiers were sent to quell the riot in the city centre.
To quell something means to stop it, especially when it is loud or strong.
He took a deep breath to quell the wave of nerves before going on stage.

entries.meaning: the power to have an effect on someone or something; (v) to have such an effect.
examples: Her older sister had a big influence on the kind of music she listened to.
The weather can have a strong influence on people's moods.
He used his influence to help the small charity get a meeting with the mayor.
To influence someone is to have an effect on what they think or do.
Books can have a powerful influence on the way young readers see the world.

entries.meaning: opposite to what you are saying or what you expect. Saying the opposite of what you really mean, often in a humorous way.
examples: It was ironic that the fire station burned down while the crew were out on a call.
"What lovely weather," he said in an ironic tone as the rain soaked his coat.
She found it ironic that the swimming instructor was afraid of deep water.
To be ironic is to say the opposite of what you mean, usually to make a point.
In an ironic twist, the thief's own car was stolen while he was robbing the shop.

entries.meaning: respecting different behaviours or beliefs; open-minded. Also giving generously or in large amounts.
examples: Her parents were liberal and allowed her to choose her own hobbies.
He spread a liberal amount of butter across his warm toast.
The school has a liberal attitude towards pupils' different customs and beliefs.
To be liberal is to accept that other people may think differently from you.
The judges were liberal with their praise for the young musician.

entries.meaning: far too much and completely unnecessary. Also given free of charge, costing nothing.
examples: The teacher removed the gratuitous violence from the story before reading it aloud.
His gratuitous remarks about her painting were unkind and served no purpose.
The hotel offered gratuitous breakfast to every guest who stayed the weekend.
Something gratuitous is either uncalled for or given without any charge.
She thought the extra decorations on the cake were gratuitous and rather silly.

entries.meaning: unable to move or doesn't react; completely still and lifeless.
examples: The injured bird lay inert on the pavement until the vet arrived.
Helium is an inert gas, which means it does not easily react with other substances.
After the long hike, he lay inert on the sofa for the rest of the evening.
Something inert neither moves nor reacts to what is around it.
The old machine stood inert in the corner of the workshop, its engine long dead.

entries.meaning: to stop something's effect or cancel it out. Also to make something negative or deny it.
examples: Eating a whole cake would negate all the exercise he had done that week.
One careless mistake can negate hours of hard work.
The scientist could not negate the results, as the evidence was too strong.
To negate something is to wipe out its effect completely.
Heavy rain on match day negated the advantage of their faster players.

entries.meaning: to satisfy a need or wish, especially thirst. Also to put out a fire with a liquid.
examples: After the long run, only cold water could quench her thirst.
The firefighters worked through the night to quench the blaze.
Nothing could quench his curiosity about how the machine worked.
To quench is to satisfy a need or to put out a fire with liquid.
He poured a bucket of sand over the campfire to quench the last of the flames.

entries.meaning: to feel very sad or to be deeply upset, especially after losing someone.
examples: The whole family gathered to grieve for their beloved grandmother.
It took him many months to grieve the loss of his old dog.
She continued to grieve quietly long after the funeral had ended.
To grieve is to feel a deep sadness that takes time to fade.
The villagers came together to grieve and to remember happier days.

entries.meaning: teaching a moral lesson. Also a fixed, rather preachy way of teaching.
examples: Aesop's fables are didactic stories that each end with a moral.
The poem was rather didactic, telling readers exactly how they ought to behave.
His didactic tone made the lesson feel more like a lecture than a discussion.
A didactic tale is written to teach a lesson as well as to entertain.
The museum guide took a didactic approach, correcting every small error.

entries.meaning: of a lower rank or position, or of poorer quality.
examples: The cheaper paint was clearly inferior and peeled within a month.
In the old army, a soldier had to obey any officer of inferior rank to the general.
She refused to feel inferior just because she was the youngest in the team.
Something inferior is either lower in rank or worse in quality.
The judges rejected the entry because the materials were of inferior quality.

entries.meaning: guesses or conclusions made using the information you already have.
examples: From the muddy footprints, the detective made several clever inferences.
In comprehension tests, pupils must draw inferences from clues in the text.
Her inferences about the ending turned out to be completely correct.
Inferences are sensible guesses built on the evidence in front of you.
Scientists drew careful inferences from the data they had collected.

entries.meaning: to unwillingly agree to something; to give in or surrender.
examples: After hours of pleading, her father finally began to capitulate about the puppy.
The exhausted army had no choice but to capitulate to the larger force.
He refused to capitulate to the bully's unfair demands.
To capitulate is to give in when you would rather not.
The company chose to capitulate and lower its prices after weeks of protest.

entries.meaning: completely unreasonable or foolish. Also suffering from a serious mental illness.
examples: Cycling down that steep hill without brakes would be an insane thing to do.
The queue for the new ride was insane, stretching right around the park.
In the old novel, the lonely character was described as insane and locked away.
Something insane is either wildly unreasonable or affected by mental illness.
He had an insane idea to build a raft out of empty plastic bottles.

entries.meaning: being united and sticking together as one.
examples: The team's cohesion improved after a weekend of training together.
Good cohesion between paragraphs makes an essay much easier to follow.
The cohesion of water droplets allows them to cling to a leaf.
Cohesion is what holds a group or a piece of writing firmly together.
Without cohesion, the choir's voices simply would not blend.

entries.meaning: behaviour that takes other people's feelings into account. Also careful thought about something.
examples: He showed great consideration by carrying his neighbour's shopping.
After much consideration, she decided to join the orchestra instead of the choir.
Please show consideration for others by keeping your voice down in the library.
Consideration means thinking of others as well as thinking carefully.
The plans were given serious consideration before the council voted.

entries.meaning: something that supports or improves, making a thing stronger.
examples: Winning the first match was a real booster for the team's confidence.
The rocket's booster fell away once it had left the atmosphere.
The nurse explained that a booster would strengthen his protection.
A booster is anything that supports something and makes it stronger.
Her kind words were a welcome booster on a very difficult day.

entries.meaning: total confusion with no order at all.
examples: When the power failed, the busy station descended into chaos.
There was complete chaos in the kitchen after the puppy got in.
The snowstorm caused chaos on the roads all morning.
Chaos is what remains when order disappears altogether.
The supply teacher struggled to bring the chaos under control.

entries.meaning: to give up a job or position. Also to give up fighting and accept something.
examples: The manager decided to resign after the club's tenth defeat.
She had to resign herself to missing the trip because of her broken ankle.
He will resign from the committee at the end of the school year.
To resign is to leave a position or to give up struggling against something.
Rather than resign, the captain promised to work harder than ever.

entries.meaning: to live in a particular place.
examples: Penguins inhabit some of the coldest places on Earth.
Only a handful of families still inhabit the tiny island.
Bats inhabit the dark caves beneath the hillside.
To inhabit somewhere is simply to live there.
Strange creatures are said to inhabit the deepest parts of the ocean.

entries.meaning: harmful or damaging to something.
examples: Too little sleep is detrimental to your concentration in lessons.
The factory's waste proved detrimental to the fish in the river.
Constant criticism can be detrimental to a young person's confidence.
Anything detrimental causes harm or damage.
The heatwave was detrimental to the farmer's entire wheat crop.

entries.meaning: careful not to use or waste something, especially money.
examples: The little car is very economical and uses hardly any fuel.
Being economical with paper means printing on both sides.
Her grandmother was economical, saving every scrap of wool for later.
To be economical is to use only what you need and waste nothing.
Cooking a large pot of soup is an economical way to feed the family.

entries.meaning: to shake slightly because of emotion, usually fear. Also a case used for carrying arrows.
examples: His bottom lip began to quiver as he stood up to read his poem aloud.
The archer pulled another arrow from the quiver on her back.
She felt her hands quiver with nerves before the piano exam began.
To quiver is to shake very slightly, often because you are frightened.
The leaves quiver whenever the smallest breeze passes through the hedge.

entries.meaning: to appear or come out of somewhere. Also for a fact to become known.
examples: The badger waited until dusk to emerge from its sett.
New details about the discovery began to emerge in the newspapers.
Divers watched the submarine slowly emerge from the murky water.
To emerge is to come out of somewhere and become visible.
A butterfly will emerge from its chrysalis when its wings are ready.

entries.meaning: to take control of a powerful position without any right to do so.
examples: The ambitious duke plotted to usurp the throne from his young nephew.
In the play, a jealous brother tries to usurp the crown.
No one may usurp the powers that belong to Parliament.
To usurp is to seize a position you have no right to hold.
The general attempted to usurp control of the government by force.

entries.meaning: suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
examples: Ominous grey clouds gathered above the campsite.
There was an ominous silence in the hall after the headteacher spoke.
The creaking of the old bridge was an ominous sound.
Something ominous is a warning sign that trouble lies ahead.
He heard an ominous rumble from the volcano in the distance.

entries.meaning: an event or person that causes lots of change. Also a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction.
examples: The new coach was the catalyst for the team's remarkable season.
Her letter proved to be the catalyst for enormous change in the village.
In the experiment, a catalyst made the reaction happen far more quickly.
A catalyst is anything that sets off a great deal of change.
The invention of the printing press acted as a catalyst for learning across Europe.

entries.meaning: to prevent or stop something from happening easily. Also a large basket for carrying food.
examples: Thick fog began to hamper the rescue team's search of the hillside.
They carried a wicker hamper filled with sandwiches to the picnic.
A heavy rucksack will hamper you on a long climb.
To hamper is to get in the way, though a hamper is also a food basket.
Constant interruptions hamper her attempts to finish her homework.

entries.meaning: a person who buys and sells items as a career; a trader.
examples: The wool merchant travelled from town to town selling his cloth.
A wealthy merchant built the grand house beside the harbour.
Merchants once sailed the Silk Road carrying spices and silk.
A merchant is somebody whose job is buying and selling goods.
She bought the timber from a local builders' merchant.

entries.meaning: a very wise person. Also wise and sensible, or a herb used in cooking.
examples: The village turned to the old sage whenever a dispute arose.
Her grandfather offered sage advice about saving money carefully.
The recipe asked for a little chopped sage and onion.
A sage is a wise person, and sage also describes wise words.
Ancient rulers often kept a sage at court to guide their decisions.

entries.meaning: to be slow in leaving. Also to continue to exist for longer than expected.
examples: The friends chose to linger by the gate, unwilling to say goodbye.
The smell of woodsmoke seemed to linger in his jumper for days.
Do not linger in the corridor once the bell has rung.
To linger is to stay behind or to last far longer than expected.
Memories of that summer holiday still linger many years later.

entries.meaning: something that seems impossible because it involves two opposite facts.
examples: It is a paradox that the more you give away, the richer you may feel.
The statement "this sentence is false" is a famous paradox.
She pointed out the paradox of a library that nobody was allowed to enter.
A paradox holds two opposite ideas that somehow both seem true.
The paradox of the crowded island is that it can still feel lonely.

entries.meaning: a place to stay on holiday, or a building where clubs meet. Also to become firmly stuck, or to make an official complaint.
examples: The family stayed in a wooden lodge beside the loch.
Members of the club gathered at the lodge every Thursday evening.
A small stone had lodged itself in the tread of his boot.
A lodge is a place to stay or meet, and to lodge is to stick fast.
Her father decided to lodge a complaint about the delayed train.

entries.meaning: flaunting money, power or possessions in a showy way to impress people.
examples: He arrived in an ostentatious gold car that everyone stopped to stare at.
The ostentatious chandelier seemed far too grand for such a small room.
She disliked ostentatious displays of wealth at family celebrations.
Ostentatious behaviour is showing off in order to impress others.
The palace was ostentatious, with marble floors in every corridor.

entries.meaning: to give a document to someone so that it can be considered. Also to give in or yield to someone.
examples: Pupils must submit their entries to the poetry competition by Friday.
The architect will submit the plans to the council next week.
The knight refused to submit, even when he was hopelessly outnumbered.
To submit is to hand something in or to give in to someone stronger.
She had to submit her application before the deadline closed.

entries.meaning: to support or approve of something publicly. Also to sign the back of a document.
examples: The famous runner agreed to endorse the new brand of trainers.
All the governors chose to endorse the headteacher's plan.
He had to endorse the cheque by signing his name on the back.
To endorse something is to give it your public support.
The charity would not endorse any product it had not tested.

entries.meaning: to live somewhere.
examples: Her cousins reside in a small cottage on the edge of the moor.
Around eight million people reside in London.
The family had resided at the same address for over fifty years.
To reside somewhere is simply to live there.
Puffins reside on the cliffs during the nesting season.

entries.meaning: to make something bigger, longer, or to stretch it out. Also to offer something such as a welcome.
examples: They plan to extend the kitchen out into the garden.
The librarian agreed to extend the loan by another two weeks.
He had to extend his arm fully to reach the top shelf.
To extend is to make something longer, larger or wider.
The head wished to extend a warm welcome to all the new pupils.

entries.meaning: beautiful, powerful, or worthy of great respect.
examples: A majestic stag stood silhouetted against the morning sky.
The majestic cathedral towered above the rooftops of the city.
They watched the majestic eagle circle high above the valley.
Something majestic is grand enough to command real respect.
The mountains looked especially majestic under a fresh fall of snow.

entries.meaning: to steal goods, usually small or inexpensive items.
examples: Someone had been pilfering biscuits from the staffroom tin.
The magpie would pilfer anything shiny it could carry away.
It is wrong to pilfer stationery from the office, however small the item.
To pilfer is to steal small things, usually a little at a time.
The shopkeeper caught the pair trying to pilfer sweets from the counter.

entries.meaning: making decisions for yourself, independently of anyone else.
examples: The region became autonomous and now makes its own laws.
Autonomous vehicles can steer and brake without a driver.
Older pupils are encouraged to become more autonomous learners.
To be autonomous is to make your own decisions without being told.
The charity remained autonomous, refusing money that came with conditions.

entries.meaning: a serious promise that you will do something.
examples: Every witness must take an oath to tell the truth in court.
The two friends swore an oath never to reveal the secret.
A new doctor takes an oath to care for every patient.
An oath is a solemn promise that should never be broken.
He kept his oath, even when it became difficult to do so.

entries.meaning: to cause things to happen; to start something off, often trouble.
examples: A single unkind comment was enough to instigate the whole argument.
The council decided to instigate a review of the town's bus routes.
He was accused of trying to instigate a rebellion among the crew.
To instigate is to be the person who causes something to begin.
Her letter helped instigate a campaign to save the local woodland.

entries.meaning: money saved or set aside for something specific. Also to provide the money for something.
examples: The school started a fund to pay for new library books.
Her parents agreed to fund half the cost of the music course.
There is an emergency fund kept aside for repairs to the village hall.
A fund is money set aside, and to fund is to pay for something.
The charity hopes to fund a new well in the drought-hit village.

entries.meaning: having a pleasant smell.
examples: The garden was fragrant with roses and honeysuckle.
A fragrant loaf of bread had just come out of the oven.
She chose a fragrant soap that smelled of lavender.
Anything fragrant gives off a pleasant, agreeable smell.
The fragrant steam from the curry filled the whole kitchen.

entries.meaning: behaving in a silly way and not taking anything seriously; not worth serious attention.
examples: The teacher had no patience for frivolous chatter during the test.
Buying a third pair of trainers seemed a frivolous use of his savings.
She asked a frivolous question just to delay the start of the lesson.
Something frivolous is silly and not worth taking seriously.
The committee dismissed the complaint as frivolous and moved on.

entries.meaning: to prevent something bad from happening. Also to turn your eyes or face away.
examples: Quick thinking by the driver helped avert a serious accident.
She had to avert her eyes from the bright glare of the welding torch.
Talks between the two countries managed to avert a war.
To avert is to prevent something bad or to turn your face aside.
He tried to avert disaster by switching the machine off at once.

entries.meaning: careful with money or food; not wasteful, and sometimes very plain or small.
examples: Her frugal habits meant she never wasted a scrap of food.
They ate a frugal supper of bread, cheese and a single apple.
Being frugal as a student allowed him to save for the trip.
A frugal person spends carefully and wastes very little.
The explorers survived on frugal rations for the final week.

entries.meaning: to work together with someone on a shared task.
examples: The two classes will collaborate on a display for the summer fair.
Scientists from six countries collaborate on the space telescope.
She agreed to collaborate with her friend on the science project.
To collaborate is to work alongside others towards the same goal.
Authors sometimes collaborate to write a single book together.

entries.meaning: thinking you are more important than other people; excessive self-importance.
examples: His egotism meant he spoke only about his own achievements.
The captain's egotism made the rest of the team feel ignored.
There is a difference between healthy confidence and plain egotism.
Egotism is believing that you matter more than everyone else.
Fame had encouraged an egotism that his old friends barely recognised.

entries.meaning: to fill up or use space or time. Also to live in a place or take control of it.
examples: The new sofa will occupy most of the far wall.
Jigsaw puzzles occupy him for hours on rainy afternoons.
The same family have occupied the farmhouse for generations.
To occupy is to fill space or time, or to live somewhere.
Enemy troops occupied the town for almost three years.

entries.meaning: a style or category of one of the arts, such as books, films or music.
examples: Mystery is her favourite genre of book.
The film blends the comedy and adventure genres.
Jazz is a musical genre that grew up in New Orleans.
A genre is simply a category of writing, music or art.
He enjoys every genre except horror.

entries.meaning: skilful and showing great intelligence, especially with your hands or your words.
examples: The adroit goalkeeper tipped the ball over the crossbar.
She gave an adroit answer that satisfied everybody in the room.
His adroit fingers repaired the tiny watch in minutes.
Someone adroit is clever and skilful at what they do.
The adroit negotiator settled the dispute before lunchtime.

entries.meaning: to leave somebody or a place, or to stop doing something. Also complete freedom from worry or care.
examples: The crew had to abandon the sinking ship in the darkness.
Heavy snow forced them to abandon the search until morning.
She danced with such abandon that she forgot everyone was watching.
To abandon is to leave or give up, while abandon also means acting without care.
Please do not abandon the project just because the first attempt failed.

entries.meaning: to rub food against a metal tool to cut it into small pieces. Also a metal frame in a fireplace, or to irritate someone.
examples: Please grate the cheese finely before sprinkling it on the pasta.
The logs crackled in the iron grate by the window.
His constant humming began to grate on everyone's nerves.
To grate is to shred food, though a grate is also part of a fireplace.
She had to grate a whole carrot for the cake mixture.

entries.meaning: an informal style of speech, often specific to one area; the way people really talk.
examples: "Owt" and "nowt" are colloquial Yorkshire words for anything and nothing.
Avoid colloquial language when writing a formal letter.
The story felt lively because it used colloquial speech for the dialogue.
Colloquial language is the informal talk people use every day.
Her essay was marked down for being too colloquial in places.

entries.meaning: to send someone away from their country forever. Also to get rid of a thought or feeling.
examples: The king chose to banish the traitor from the kingdom for life.
She tried to banish all thoughts of failure before the race.
In the fairy tale, the witch is banished to a distant island.
To banish is to send away for good or to drive a feeling out.
A hot drink helped banish the chill from his fingers.

entries.meaning: respected, famous and important in a particular field.
examples: An eminent surgeon travelled from London to perform the operation.
The lecture was given by an eminent historian of the Roman period.
She hopes one day to become an eminent marine biologist.
Someone eminent is well known and highly respected for their work.
Several eminent guests were invited to open the new museum.

entries.meaning: a long and serious talk or essay about a subject. Also to speak or write about something at length.
examples: The professor delivered a lengthy discourse on ancient Greek pottery.
Their discourse about the future of the club lasted well past midnight.
He would happily discourse on trains to anybody who would listen.
A discourse is a long, serious discussion or piece of writing.
Public discourse about the new road grew more heated each week.

entries.meaning: very serious. Also a place where somebody is buried.
examples: The doctor wore a grave expression as she read the results.
Ignoring the warning signs would be a grave mistake.
They laid flowers on the grave of the unknown soldier.
Grave means very serious, but a grave is also a burial place.
The country faces a grave shortage of clean water.

entries.meaning: money borrowed or the ability to borrow. Also praise or honour given to someone.
examples: She deserves credit for finishing the race despite her injury.
The shop allows customers to buy the sofa on credit.
The film's credits listed everyone who had worked on it.
Credit can mean borrowed money or the praise you are owed.
He was too modest to credit himself with the team's success.

entries.meaning: to act in line with an order, a set of rules, or a request.
examples: All visitors must comply with the safety rules in the laboratory.
He refused to comply with such an unreasonable demand.
The factory was closed until it agreed to comply with the new regulations.
To comply is to do as the rules or instructions say.
She asked politely, and everyone was happy to comply.

entries.meaning: a word made up of two or more words. Also a mixture of two or more things, or to make a problem worse.
examples: "Football" is a compound word made from "foot" and "ball".
Water is a compound formed from hydrogen and oxygen.
Arriving late would only compound his troubles.
A compound joins two things together, and to compound a problem is to make it worse.
The class practised writing compound sentences using connectives.

entries.meaning: a large feather. Also a mass of smoke, dust or water rising into the air.
examples: The knight's helmet was decorated with a scarlet plume.
A plume of thick black smoke rose above the burning barn.
The volcano sent a plume of ash high into the sky.
A plume is a large feather or a rising cloud of smoke or dust.
The peacock spread its magnificent plumes to impress its mate.

entries.meaning: birds that are bred for their meat and eggs, such as chickens, ducks and turkeys.
examples: The farmer keeps poultry in a large shed behind the barn.
Poultry must be cooked thoroughly before it is safe to eat.
Ducks, geese and turkeys all count as poultry.
Poultry are birds kept for their meat and their eggs.
The market stall sold fresh poultry every Saturday morning.

entries.meaning: following the traditional or normal way of doing things.
examples: They chose a conventional white wedding cake rather than anything unusual.
The scientist's ideas challenged conventional thinking about the planets.
He took the conventional route to school instead of the shortcut.
Conventional means doing things the normal, traditional way.
Her painting style is far from conventional, which is why it stands out.

entries.meaning: at the opening or beginning of a new period, or marking the first of something.
examples: The president gave her inaugural speech to a huge crowd.
The club's inaugural meeting was held in the village hall.
Tickets sold out for the inaugural flight to the new airport.
Something inaugural marks the very beginning of something new.
He scored in the inaugural match of the competition.

entries.meaning: to please someone, or to satisfy a need or wish.
examples: It would gratify her grandmother to receive a handwritten letter.
He refused to gratify their curiosity about where he had been.
A cold drink did much to gratify their thirst after the walk.
To gratify is to please someone or to satisfy a wish.
The results were gratifying after so many months of practice.

entries.meaning: to cause something to continue, often for a very long time.
examples: Repeating the rumour only helps to perpetuate it.
The statue was built to perpetuate the memory of the explorer.
Unfair rules can perpetuate the very problems they were meant to solve.
To perpetuate something is to make it carry on and on.
The family perpetuate the tradition by meeting every New Year.

entries.meaning: something or someone that annoys you or causes trouble.
examples: The dripping tap was a constant nuisance all night long.
Wasps can be a real nuisance at a summer picnic.
He apologised for being such a nuisance during the meeting.
A nuisance is anything that annoys or gets in your way.
Losing the key was a nuisance rather than a disaster.

entries.meaning: happening often. Also to visit a place regularly.
examples: There are frequent buses into town on a Saturday.
His frequent absences meant he fell behind with the work.
The artists frequent a small café near the river.
Frequent means happening often, and to frequent a place is to go there regularly.
Frequent showers are forecast for the rest of the week.

entries.meaning: imaginary and suggested only for the sake of discussion; not real.
examples: The teacher asked a hypothetical question about life on Mars.
In a hypothetical situation, what would you do if you found a wallet?
His worries were hypothetical, since nothing had actually gone wrong.
Something hypothetical is imagined purely for the sake of argument.
The debate began with a hypothetical case rather than a real one.

entries.meaning: to care for something or somebody to help it develop and grow.
examples: She worked hard to nurture the seedlings through the cold spring.
Good teachers nurture the talents of every child in the class.
The birds nurture their chicks until they are ready to fly.
To nurture is to care for something so that it can grow.
Scientists still debate how much of our character comes from nature and how much from nurture.

entries.meaning: a strange or unusual way of behaving that belongs to one person.
examples: Tapping his pencil three times before writing was a curious idiosyncrasy.
Every member of the family had some small idiosyncrasy.
Her habit of naming every houseplant is a harmless idiosyncrasy.
An idiosyncrasy is an unusual habit that makes a person different.
The old car had an idiosyncrasy: it would only start in second gear.

entries.meaning: done with too much speed, and therefore often careless.
examples: A hasty decision at the crossroads sent them miles out of their way.
He ate a hasty breakfast and ran for the bus.
She later regretted her hasty words to her sister.
Something hasty is done in too much of a hurry to be done well.
The report was hasty and full of spelling mistakes.

entries.meaning: the force caused by two things rubbing together. Also disagreement between people.
examples: Friction between the brake pads and the wheel slows the bicycle down.
Rubbing two sticks together creates enough friction to make heat.
There was growing friction between the two departments.
Friction is the force of rubbing, but it also means a clash between people.
Oil is used to reduce friction inside the engine.

entries.meaning: to govern or treat people cruelly by taking away their freedom.
