examples: The harsh new laws were designed to oppress anyone who disagreed.
For years the dictator continued to oppress his own people.
No government should oppress those it is meant to serve.
To oppress is to rule cruelly and take away people's freedom.
The novel describes how the villagers were oppressed by the landowner.

entries.meaning: to hide something so that people cannot find it or know about it.
examples: He tried to conceal the birthday present behind his back.
Thick ivy concealed the entrance to the old cellar.
She could not conceal her delight when the letter arrived.
To conceal is to hide something from sight or from knowledge.
The chameleon can conceal itself against almost any background.

entries.meaning: to give all your time and effort to something.
examples: She plans to devote the summer to learning the violin.
He devoted his whole career to protecting seabirds.
They devote one evening a week to helping at the food bank.
To devote yourself to something is to give it all your time and effort.
The museum devotes an entire floor to Ancient Egypt.

entries.meaning: dishonest and using tricks to get what you want. Also winding or indirect.
examples: The villain hatched a devious plan to steal the trophy.
He took a devious route through the back lanes to avoid the traffic.
Her devious excuse fooled nobody for very long.
Someone devious is dishonest and uses tricks to get their way.
It was devious of him to blame the mistake on his younger brother.

entries.meaning: an aim or goal. Also fair and without bias, based on facts rather than feelings.
examples: Their main objective was to finish the raft before nightfall.
A good referee must remain objective, however loud the crowd becomes.
The report gave an objective account of what had happened.
An objective is an aim, and to be objective is to judge fairly on the facts.
She set herself the objective of reading fifty books that year.

entries.meaning: a belief that is not in line with an accepted religion. Also an opinion that goes strongly against what most people believe.
examples: In the Middle Ages, people could be punished for heresy.
Galileo's claim that the Earth moved was treated as heresy at the time.
Suggesting the team should change its badge was regarded as heresy by the fans.
Heresy is a belief that goes against the accepted religion or opinion.
The historian explained how ideas once called heresy later became ordinary science.

entries.meaning: to make someone believe something that is not true.
examples: He tried to deceive his parents about how long he had spent on the computer.
The magician's mirrors are designed to deceive the audience completely.
Do not let the calm sea deceive you, for the current is very strong.
To deceive someone is to make them believe something untrue.
She would never deceive a friend, however awkward the truth might be.

entries.meaning: detailed and complicated in design or planning. Also to explain something in greater detail.
examples: The cake was decorated with an elaborate pattern of sugar flowers.
They made elaborate plans for the school's summer production.
Could you elaborate on that idea so the rest of us understand it?
Elaborate means detailed and complicated, or to explain more fully.
The palace ceiling was covered in elaborate carvings.

entries.meaning: weak or lacking strength.
examples: The kitten gave a feeble cry from beneath the hedge.
After the illness his grip was still rather feeble.
That was a feeble excuse and nobody believed it.
Anything feeble lacks strength or force.
A feeble light flickered at the far end of the tunnel.

entries.meaning: kind, courteous and polite, especially towards guests.
examples: Their host was gracious enough to wait until everybody had arrived.
She was gracious in defeat and congratulated the winner warmly.
A gracious thank-you letter arrived the following week.
Being gracious means treating others with kindness and courtesy.
The elderly couple offered a gracious welcome to the new neighbours.

entries.meaning: to make it difficult for something to happen; to get in the way.
examples: Deep snow began to hinder the progress of the mountain rescue team.
A noisy classroom can hinder concentration.
His broken wrist did not hinder him from finishing the puzzle.
To hinder is to make something harder to do.
Roadworks will hinder traffic through the town all summer.

entries.meaning: not favouring one side or another; completely fair.
examples: A referee must remain impartial even when the crowd disagrees.
The judges gave an impartial decision based only on the evidence.
She tried to be impartial when her two friends argued.
To be impartial is to treat every side equally fairly.
An impartial report should not favour either party.

entries.meaning: cheerful and friendly.
examples: Their jovial uncle kept everyone laughing throughout the meal.
A jovial atmosphere filled the hall on the last day of term.
He gave a jovial wave as he cycled past the window.
Someone jovial is cheerful and easy to be around.
The jovial shopkeeper knew every customer by name.

entries.meaning: similar in nature, or related by family or character.
examples: The two girls were kindred spirits who both loved astronomy.
He travelled north to meet kindred he had never known.
Wolves and dogs are kindred creatures.
Kindred means alike in nature or joined by family.
They found kindred interests in music and long walks.

entries.meaning: of only average quality; not exceptional in any way.
examples: The film was mediocre, neither dreadful nor especially good.
He was disappointed with his mediocre score in the test.
A mediocre meal spoiled an otherwise perfect evening.
Something mediocre is merely average and nothing more.
The team's mediocre season ended in mid-table.

entries.meaning: to fail to care for something properly, or to leave it undone.
examples: Never neglect a pet, however busy you happen to be.
Years of neglect had left the old cottage crumbling.
He did not neglect his homework even during the holidays.
To neglect something is to fail to look after it.
The garden showed signs of neglect after the long winter.

entries.meaning: not aware of or not concerned about what is happening around you.
examples: Lost in her book, she was oblivious to the noise around her.
He walked on, oblivious of the puddle directly ahead.
The sleeping cat was oblivious to the thunderstorm outside.
To be oblivious is to notice nothing of what is going on.
They were oblivious to how late it had become.

entries.meaning: having a high status or reputation; greatly admired.
examples: She won a prestigious award for her science project.
The orchestra performed at one of the most prestigious halls in Europe.
A prestigious university offered him a place immediately.
Something prestigious carries great respect and reputation.
Winning that prestigious cup had been the club's dream for years.

entries.meaning: to satisfy a thirst, or to extinguish something such as a fire.
examples: A jug of cold lemonade helped quench their thirst in the heat.
Sand was thrown over the embers to quench them completely.
Nothing could quench her determination to learn the piece.
To quench is to satisfy thirst or to put something out.
The heavy downpour quenched the last of the moorland fire.

entries.meaning: acting without thinking about the consequences; rash and careless.
examples: It was reckless to cycle down the hill without brakes.
The driver was fined for reckless overtaking on the bend.
Her reckless spending left nothing for the school trip.
Reckless behaviour ignores the dangers completely.
He made a reckless promise he could not possibly keep.

entries.meaning: not moving or flowing; inactive and going nowhere.
examples: Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water, so the pond was drained.
The stagnant ditch gave off a very unpleasant smell.
Sales remained stagnant throughout the wet summer.
Something stagnant neither moves nor changes.
After a stagnant first half, the match burst into life.

entries.meaning: shy or lacking confidence.
examples: The timid mouse darted back beneath the floorboards.
She gave a timid knock at the headteacher's door.
He was too timid to volunteer, though he knew the answer.
Someone timid is shy and short of confidence.
A timid smile crossed the new boy's face.

entries.meaning: present or appearing everywhere.
examples: Mobile phones have become ubiquitous in modern life.
Seagulls are ubiquitous along that stretch of coast.
The ubiquitous smell of baking drifted through every street.
Something ubiquitous seems to turn up absolutely everywhere.
Plastic packaging is unfortunately ubiquitous in our shops.

entries.meaning: strong, healthy and full of energy.
examples: A vigorous jog around the park woke him up properly.
The young sapling made vigorous growth in the spring rain.
She gave a vigorous defence of her argument in the debate.
Vigorous means strong, healthy and bursting with energy.
Vigorous scrubbing finally removed the stain from the carpet.

entries.meaning: showing quick and inventive humour.
examples: His witty reply had the whole class laughing.
The play was full of witty remarks about village life.
She is famous for her witty descriptions of everyday things.
Someone witty is quick and clever at being funny.
A witty caption made the photograph even better.

entries.meaning: full of happiness and joy.
examples: They spent a blissful afternoon reading beside the river.
A blissful silence fell once the drilling finally stopped.
The blissful smile on her face said everything.
Something blissful is full of pure happiness.
He remembered a blissful summer spent at his grandparents' farm.

entries.meaning: to confuse or puzzle someone completely.
examples: The final question in the maths paper seemed to perplex everybody.
It continued to perplex him that the door had been left unlocked.
Riddles are designed to perplex the listener before delighting them.
To perplex someone is to leave them thoroughly puzzled.
Her sudden change of mind perplexed the whole family.

entries.meaning: charmingly old-fashioned or unusual.
examples: They stayed in a quaint cottage with roses around the door.
The village has a quaint custom of racing cheeses down the hill.
Her grandmother used quaint expressions nobody says any more.
Something quaint is charming because it is old-fashioned.
The quaint little bookshop was hidden down a cobbled lane.

entries.meaning: to deeply respect or admire someone or something.
examples: Musicians across the world revere her recordings.
The village came to revere the doctor who had served them for forty years.
Many cultures revere the memory of their ancestors.
To revere someone is to hold them in the deepest respect.
He revered his grandfather above anyone else he knew.

entries.meaning: not easily convinced; having doubts about something.
examples: She was sceptical about his claim to have seen a shooting star.
Scientists remained sceptical until the results were repeated.
His sceptical expression showed he did not believe a word.
To be sceptical is to have doubts and want more proof.
The class grew sceptical of every advert they were shown.

entries.meaning: calm, peaceful and quiet.
examples: The lake was tranquil in the early morning light.
They found a tranquil corner of the garden to read in.
Nothing disturbed the tranquil silence of the empty church.
Something tranquil is calm, quiet and untroubled.
After the storm the sea became strangely tranquil.

entries.meaning: fully in agreement, with everyone sharing the same opinion.
examples: The vote was unanimous, with every hand raised.
There was unanimous praise for the school choir.
The judges reached a unanimous decision within minutes.
Unanimous means that absolutely everybody agrees.
The committee gave unanimous support to the new playground.

entries.meaning: able to adapt to many different functions or activities.
examples: A versatile player, she can play in almost any position.
Eggs are a versatile ingredient used in hundreds of dishes.
The versatile tool folds out into a knife, a saw and a screwdriver.
Something versatile can be used in many different ways.
He is a versatile musician who plays five instruments.

entries.meaning: good for your health, morally sound, or generally beneficial.
examples: They ate a wholesome supper of soup and fresh bread.
The programme was wholesome family entertainment.
Long walks in the fresh air are thoroughly wholesome.
Something wholesome is good for the body or the character.
She remembered the wholesome food her grandmother used to cook.

entries.meaning: to have a strong desire or longing for something.
examples: After a month at sea the sailors began to yearn for home.
She would yearn for the summer holidays all through February.
Many people yearn for a simpler, quieter life.
To yearn is to want something very deeply indeed.
He yearned to see his old friends once more.

entries.meaning: having great enthusiasm or passion for a cause.
examples: She is a zealous supporter of the campaign to save the woods.
His zealous training paid off at the county championships.
The zealous volunteers cleared the whole beach in one morning.
Someone zealous is full of passion for what they believe in.
Their zealous efforts raised more money than anyone expected.

entries.meaning: full of energy and life; bright and striking.
examples: The market was a vibrant mix of colours, smells and voices.
She chose a vibrant orange for her bedroom wall.
The city has a vibrant music scene.
Something vibrant is bright and bursting with life.
Vibrant poppies covered the whole hillside.

entries.meaning: very detailed and complicated.
examples: The clock contained an intricate arrangement of tiny cogs.
She admired the intricate lace on the old christening gown.
The plot of the novel is intricate but rewarding.
Something intricate has many small, detailed parts.
An intricate pattern of frost covered the window pane.

entries.meaning: strong and healthy; vigorous and sturdy.
examples: The robust little boat rode out the storm without damage.
Despite his age, her grandfather remains remarkably robust.
The bridge needs a robust design to carry heavy lorries.
Something robust is strong enough to stand hard use.
She gave a robust defence of her team's performance.

entries.meaning: careful to avoid possible problems or dangers.
examples: He took a cautious step onto the frozen pond.
Her cautious approach meant she never lost her savings.
The vet gave a cautious welcome to the puppy's recovery.
Being cautious means taking care to avoid danger.
A cautious driver slows down long before the junction.

entries.meaning: fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing.
examples: Her eloquent speech convinced the whole council.
He wrote an eloquent letter in defence of the library.
The eloquent lawyer held the courtroom's attention.
Someone eloquent speaks or writes clearly and persuasively.
An eloquent silence followed the announcement.

entries.meaning: shining faintly with a wavering, unsteady light.
examples: A glimmering candle was the only light in the room.
They followed the glimmering lights of the village home.
Stars were glimmering faintly through the thin cloud.
Something glimmering shines with a faint, wavering light.
The glimmering surface of the canal reflected the lamps.

entries.meaning: having or showing impressive beauty or dignity.
examples: A majestic oak stood at the centre of the park.
They watched the majestic ship glide out of the harbour.
The organ filled the cathedral with majestic music.
Something majestic is grand and full of dignity.
Snow made the whole valley look majestic that morning.

entries.meaning: completely baffling and very puzzling.
examples: The disappearance of the keys was most perplexing.
She stared at the perplexing instructions for the flat-pack shelf.
It is perplexing that the plant grows only in that one field.
Something perplexing leaves you thoroughly puzzled.
The detective faced the most perplexing case of her career.

entries.meaning: calm, peaceful and untroubled.
examples: She remained serene even as the deadline approached.
The serene surface of the lake mirrored the mountains.
A serene expression settled on the sleeping baby's face.
Someone serene stays calm and untroubled.
They spent a serene evening watching the sun go down.

entries.meaning: playfully quaint or fanciful, especially in an appealing way.
examples: The garden was full of whimsical statues of dancing hares.
She wrote a whimsical story about a postbox that could talk.
His whimsical sense of humour delighted the younger children.
Something whimsical is playful and delightfully odd.
The café had a whimsical ceiling painted with upside-down umbrellas.

entries.meaning: to go up or climb.
examples: The walkers began to ascend the steep path before dawn.
Hot air balloons ascend as the air inside them is heated.
She watched the lift ascend to the top floor.
To ascend is to move upwards or climb.
The eagle ascended until it was only a speck in the sky.

entries.meaning: to support or strengthen something. Also a long, firm pillow.
examples: A win in the first round would bolster the team's confidence.
Extra beams were added to bolster the roof of the barn.
He propped himself up against a long bolster to read.
To bolster is to support something and make it stronger.
The evidence helped bolster her side of the argument.

entries.meaning: to prepare and use land for crops or gardening. Also to develop a skill or friendship.
examples: The family cultivate three fields of barley each year.
She began to cultivate a small vegetable patch behind the shed.
It takes time to cultivate a genuine friendship.
To cultivate is to work the land or to develop something carefully.
Monks once cultivated herbs in the garden beside the abbey.

entries.meaning: to show something clearly and deliberately. Also to take part in a public protest.
examples: The teacher will demonstrate the experiment before the class tries it.
His results demonstrate that the plants grow faster in warmth.
Hundreds gathered to demonstrate against the closure of the pool.
To demonstrate is to show something clearly on purpose.
She demonstrated the new dance step twice, very slowly.

entries.meaning: to make an action or process easier.
examples: The new bridge will facilitate travel between the two villages.
Clear instructions facilitate learning for everyone in the class.
A librarian is there to facilitate your research, not to do it for you.
To facilitate something is to make it easier to do.
Ramps were installed to facilitate access to the building.

entries.meaning: to light something up. Also to make something clearer or easier to understand.
examples: Hundreds of candles illuminate the hall at Christmas.
A single lamp illuminated the corner of the workshop.
Her explanation helped illuminate a difficult passage in the poem.
To illuminate is to light something up or to make it clear.
Lightning illuminated the whole valley for a moment.

entries.meaning: to try to reach an agreement or compromise. Also to get past a difficult obstacle.
examples: The two countries met to negotiate a peace treaty.
She had to negotiate a fair price for the second-hand bicycle.
The lorry struggled to negotiate the narrow bend.
To negotiate is to talk in order to reach an agreement.
Pupils negotiated the rules of the game before starting.

entries.meaning: to succeed in dealing with a problem or difficulty.
examples: She worked hard to overcome her fear of deep water.
The team overcame a two-goal deficit to win the match.
He overcame every obstacle on the way to the summit.
To overcome is to succeed against a problem or difficulty.
They were overcome with joy at the good news.

entries.meaning: to give new life or energy to something.
examples: A short nap can revitalise you before an evening of homework.
The council hopes to revitalise the old market square.
Rain revitalised the parched lawns after weeks of drought.
To revitalise is to give something fresh life and energy.
New members revitalised the struggling chess club.

entries.meaning: to make a thorough or dramatic change in form or appearance.
examples: A caterpillar will transform into a butterfly.
Fresh paint completely transformed the dingy classroom.
The internet has transformed the way people work.
To transform is to change something dramatically.
Snow transformed the ordinary street into something magical.

entries.meaning: an unusual and exciting experience or activity.
examples: Their camping trip turned into a real adventure when the map blew away.
She reads books about adventure in the polar regions.
Every holiday with his cousins was an adventure.
An adventure is an exciting and unusual experience.
The old sailor told tales of adventure on distant seas.

entries.meaning: a strong desire to know or learn something. Also an unusual or interesting object.
examples: Her curiosity led her to read everything she could about volcanoes.
Curiosity got the better of him and he opened the box.
The museum displayed several curiosities collected by Victorian travellers.
Curiosity is the strong wish to find out about something.
A scientist's curiosity is the beginning of every discovery.

entries.meaning: intense and eager enjoyment or interest.
examples: She threw herself into rehearsals with great enthusiasm.
His enthusiasm for astronomy was obvious to everyone.
The class greeted the trip with noisy enthusiasm.
Enthusiasm is eager interest and enjoyment.
Nothing could dampen their enthusiasm, not even the rain.

entries.meaning: a pleasing arrangement of parts; agreement and peace between people.
examples: The choir sang the final verse in beautiful harmony.
The neighbours have lived in harmony for over twenty years.
There is real harmony between the colours in that painting.
Harmony is when parts fit pleasingly together, or people agree.
She wants to live in harmony with the natural world.

entries.meaning: a new method, idea or product.
examples: The printing press was an innovation that changed the world.
The company is known for innovation in recycling.
Her innovation was a simple clip that stopped the wire tangling.
An innovation is a new idea, method or invention.
Innovation in medicine has saved countless lives.

entries.meaning: the act of travelling from one place to another.
examples: The journey to the coast took nearly four hours.
They journeyed north in search of the puffin colony.
Her journey to becoming a doctor began with a school science club.
A journey is the act of travelling from place to place.
He read the whole book during the train journey.

entries.meaning: something that is difficult or impossible to understand or explain.
examples: The disappearance of the ship remains a complete mystery.
It is a mystery to me how he finished so quickly.
She loves reading a good mystery on a rainy afternoon.
A mystery is something nobody can properly explain.
The stone circle's purpose is still something of a mystery.

entries.meaning: persistence in doing something despite difficulty or delay.
examples: Her perseverance finally earned her a place in the orchestra.
Learning an instrument takes real perseverance.
Perseverance, not luck, got the team through the final round.
Perseverance means keeping going even when things are hard.
The explorer's perseverance carried her across the ice cap.

entries.meaning: a wide range or variety of something. Also the band of colours seen in a rainbow.
examples: The survey collected views from across the whole spectrum of the school.
A prism splits white light into the spectrum of colours.
Her interests cover a broad spectrum, from fossils to football.
A spectrum is a wide range, or the colours of the rainbow.
Opinions on the matter ran the full spectrum from delight to fury.

entries.meaning: the quality of having experience, knowledge and good judgement.
examples: Her grandmother's wisdom guided the family through hard times.
It takes wisdom to know when to speak and when to listen.
He questioned the wisdom of setting out in such poor weather.
Wisdom is knowledge and experience joined to good judgement.
Ancient tales are often full of quiet wisdom.

entries.meaning: the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles. Also the state of being whole and undamaged.
examples: The referee was known throughout the league for her integrity.
He showed real integrity by admitting the mistake was his.
Engineers checked the integrity of the bridge after the flood.
Integrity means being honest, and also being whole and sound.
A person of integrity does the right thing even when nobody is watching.

entries.meaning: the ability to recover quickly from difficulties.
examples: Her resilience after the injury impressed the whole squad.
Children often show remarkable resilience in difficult times.
The resilience of the little tree amazed the gardener.
Resilience is the ability to bounce back from hardship.
Learning from failure builds resilience for the future.

entries.meaning: a strong desire to achieve something.
examples: Her ambition is to become a marine biologist.
His ambition drove him to practise every single morning.
The club has an ambition to reach the national final.
An ambition is something you badly want to achieve.
There is no harm in ambition, provided you stay kind along the way.

entries.meaning: sympathy and concern for the suffering of others.
examples: She showed great compassion towards the injured fox.
The nurse treated every patient with compassion.
His compassion for others made him a natural volunteer.
Compassion is caring deeply about somebody else's suffering.
A little compassion can change somebody's whole day.

entries.meaning: a strong desire to learn or know something.
examples: Curiosity about the stars led him to join the astronomy club.
Her endless curiosity meant she asked question after question.
Curiosity is what makes a good scientist keep looking.
Curiosity is the strong wish to learn or find out.
He opened the dusty book out of pure curiosity.

entries.meaning: the state of being equal, especially in status or rights.
examples: The school council campaigned for equality in sports funding.
Equality means everyone is treated with the same respect.
Many people fought for equality before the law.
Equality is the state of having the same rights and status.
The new rules brought greater equality between the two teams.

entries.meaning: hopefulness and confidence about the future.
examples: Despite the score, there was optimism in the changing room.
Her optimism lifted everyone's spirits on the long walk.
There is real optimism that the badgers will return.
Optimism is feeling hopeful and confident about what lies ahead.
He faced the new school year with quiet optimism.

entries.meaning: the way one understands or interprets something. Also the ability to notice things.
examples: The photograph changed her perception of the village entirely.
His perception of the problem was quite different from mine.
Owls have extremely sharp perception in the dark.
Perception is how you see and understand something.
Public perception of the plan improved once it was explained.

entries.meaning: the quality of being determined and persistent.
examples: It was tenacity rather than talent that won her the place.
The little terrier showed great tenacity in the tug-of-war.
His tenacity meant he never once missed a training session.
Tenacity is refusing to give up, however hard things become.
The rescue team's tenacity saved the stranded climbers.

entries.meaning: behaviour showing high moral standards. Also a good quality or advantage.
examples: Patience is a virtue, especially when queueing.
The story praises the virtue of telling the truth.
One virtue of the smaller car is how little fuel it uses.
Virtue is good moral behaviour, or a valuable quality.
She lived a life of quiet virtue and generosity.

entries.meaning: cheerful and full of energy.
examples: The ebullient puppy bounced around the whole kitchen.
She was ebullient after hearing she had won a place.
An ebullient crowd filled the stadium before kick-off.
Someone ebullient is bubbling over with cheerful energy.
His ebullient mood was impossible to ignore.

entries.meaning: bright or shining, especially in the dark.
examples: The hands of the old watch were luminous in the dark.
A luminous full moon lit the whole path home.
She wore a luminous jacket for cycling at dusk.
Something luminous gives off or reflects a bright light.
Luminous jellyfish drifted below the surface of the sea.

entries.meaning: representing the most perfect or typical example of something.
examples: Cream teas are the quintessential English summer treat.
He is the quintessential village cricketer.
The painting is the quintessential example of her later style.
Something quintessential is the most perfect example of its kind.
Rain at a picnic is quintessential British luck.

entries.meaning: having or showing great energy and enthusiasm.
examples: A zealous helper, she arrived an hour before anyone else.
He was zealous in his efforts to recycle everything possible.
The zealous gardener weeded every last corner of the plot.
Being zealous means throwing all your energy into something.
Their zealous practice showed in the final performance.

entries.meaning: in the form of a cloud or haze; unclear and vague.
examples: His plans for the summer were still rather nebulous.
A nebulous mist hung over the fields at dawn.
She had only a nebulous memory of the house.
Something nebulous is hazy and hard to make out.
The instructions were so nebulous that nobody knew where to start.

entries.meaning: truthful and straightforward; saying exactly what you think.
examples: To be candid, I did not enjoy the film at all.
Her candid answer surprised the interviewer.
He gave a candid account of what had gone wrong.
Being candid means being completely honest and open.
The photographer prefers candid pictures to posed ones.

entries.meaning: intimidating or overwhelming; making you feel nervous about trying.
examples: The first day at a new school can be daunting.
A daunting pile of revision waited on his desk.
The climb looked daunting from the bottom of the valley.
Something daunting seems so big that it puts you off.
She found the audition less daunting than she had feared.

entries.meaning: pointless or ineffective; certain to fail.
examples: It was futile to argue with the referee once he had decided.
Their futile attempts to start the engine lasted an hour.
Bailing out the boat with a teacup proved futile.
Something futile has no chance of achieving anything.
He made one last, futile search for his missing glove.

entries.meaning: brave, heroic, or chivalrous and polite.
examples: The gallant knight rode out to defend the village.
Despite the defeat, it had been a gallant effort.
He made a gallant attempt to carry all the bags at once.
Gallant means brave, and also courteous and chivalrous.
Her gallant rescue of the kitten made the local paper.

entries.meaning: done quickly and without much thought.
examples: He hastily scribbled a note and pushed it under the door.
The tent was hastily pitched as the rain began.
She hastily agreed, then wished she had thought it over.
To do something hastily is to do it fast and without care.
They hastily packed the picnic before the tide came in.

entries.meaning: lacking brightness or interest; drearily dull.
examples: The waiting room was painted a drab shade of grey.
February can feel like a rather drab month.
She brightened the drab hallway with a vase of tulips.
Something drab is dull and lacking any colour or interest.
His drab overcoat made him hard to spot in the crowd.

entries.meaning: behaving in a way that shows you are unhappy or worried.
examples: The fretful baby would not settle all evening.
She grew fretful as the results were read out.
A fretful night of thunder left everybody tired.
Someone fretful seems worried and unable to settle.
He gave a fretful glance at the clock every few minutes.

entries.meaning: full of danger or risk.
examples: The climbers faced a perilous descent in the fading light.
Crossing the flooded ford would have been perilous.
It was a perilous journey across the frozen lake.
Something perilous is full of danger.
The ship took a perilous course between the rocks.

entries.meaning: a person who trains wild animals.
examples: The lion tamer stepped calmly into the ring.
A horse tamer worked patiently with the nervous foal.
In the old circus, the tamer was always the star attraction.
A tamer is somebody whose job is training wild animals.
The tamer used kindness rather than force to win the animal's trust.

entries.meaning: to fall or drop straight down at high speed.
examples: The peregrine falcon can plummet faster than any other bird.
Temperatures plummet once the sun goes down in the desert.
She watched the conker plummet from the highest branch.
To plummet is to fall very fast and very steeply.
Ticket sales plummeted after the bad review.

entries.meaning: deserving praise and commendation.
examples: Raising so much for charity was a laudable achievement.
Her laudable effort to include everyone did not go unnoticed.
It is laudable to admit when you have made a mistake.
Something laudable deserves to be praised.
The club's laudable aim is to teach every child to swim.

entries.meaning: careless and unsystematic; excessively casual. Also wet and messy.
examples: His sloppy handwriting cost him marks in the test.
Sloppy work in the laboratory can ruin an experiment.
The porridge was far too sloppy to eat with a fork.
Something sloppy is careless, untidy or messily wet.
She apologised for the sloppy tidying and started again.

entries.meaning: savagely cruel; exceedingly brutal.
examples: The history book described some barbaric punishments from long ago.
It would be barbaric to leave an animal out in such weather.
The barbaric attack shocked the whole kingdom in the story.
Something barbaric is savagely cruel.
Many old laws now seem barbaric to us.

entries.meaning: bad-tempered and irritable.
examples: He is always grouchy before his morning cup of tea.
The grouchy caretaker grumbled about the muddy footprints.
Missing breakfast made her grouchy all morning.
Someone grouchy is bad-tempered and easily annoyed.
Even the grouchy neighbour smiled at the puppy.

entries.meaning: walking or moving wearily or reluctantly, often for a long way.
examples: They spent the afternoon traipsing from shop to shop.
She was tired of traipsing across the muddy field twice a day.
The children came traipsing in with soaking wet socks.
Traipsing means walking wearily or unwillingly.
He went traipsing after his brother, grumbling all the way.

entries.meaning: having or showing the ability to speak fluently and clearly. Also to express something in words.
examples: She is an articulate speaker who never loses her audience.
He struggled to articulate exactly why he felt uneasy.
The articulate young debater impressed all the judges.
Articulate means speaking clearly, or putting something into words.
Try to articulate your idea in a single sentence.

entries.meaning: giving pleasure or satisfaction.
examples: It was gratifying to see the seeds finally sprout.
Her improvement in maths was gratifying for the whole family.
There is something gratifying about a tidy desk.
Something gratifying gives real pleasure or satisfaction.
The applause at the end was deeply gratifying.

entries.meaning: pleasantly smooth or soft and free from harshness. Also to become gentler with age.
examples: The mellow notes of the cello filled the hall.
Autumn brought mellow sunshine and long shadows.
His temper had mellowed considerably over the years.
Mellow means smooth and gentle, without any harshness.
She likes the mellow flavour of properly ripened cheese.

entries.meaning: an increase or revival after a period of little activity.
examples: There has been a resurgence of interest in board games.
The resurgence of the otter population delighted conservationists.
A resurgence of energy carried her through the final mile.
A resurgence is a strong return after a quiet period.
The town saw a resurgence once the new railway opened.

entries.meaning: having or showing sensitivity in dealing with other people.
examples: She found a tactful way of telling him the news.
It was tactful of him not to mention the burnt cake.
A tactful teacher corrects mistakes without embarrassing anyone.
Being tactful means handling people's feelings with care.
His tactful silence saved the whole evening.

entries.meaning: lacking in movement, action or change. Also crackling interference on a radio.
examples: The number of visitors has remained static for three years.
A static display of costumes filled the museum's main hall.
Static crackled through the old radio during the storm.
Static means unmoving and unchanging.
Rubbing a balloon on your jumper creates static electricity.

entries.meaning: an organised massacre or violent attack, especially on a particular ethnic group.
examples: The history lesson explained how families fled a pogrom in their homeland.
Many refugees arrived in Britain having survived a pogrom.
A pogrom is a deliberate and organised attack on a group of people.
Historians study how a pogrom is planned and why it is allowed to happen.
The museum records the names of those lost in the pogrom.

entries.meaning: a person who lives in solitude, often for religious or spiritual reasons.
examples: The old hermit lived in a stone hut on the hillside.
Legend says a hermit once guarded the holy well.
Since the exams began he has become something of a hermit.
A hermit is somebody who chooses to live alone.
The hermit crab carries a borrowed shell on its back.

entries.meaning: instigating or stirring up undesirable feelings or actions.
examples: He was accused of fomenting trouble between the two classes.
The article was blamed for fomenting fear about the new road.
Fomenting an argument is far easier than ending one.
Fomenting means stirring up bad feeling or unrest.
She refused to take part in fomenting the quarrel.

entries.meaning: proceeding at a moderate pace, faster than a walk.
examples: The pony came trotting eagerly across the paddock.
She was soon trotting along beside her older sister.
The little dog went trotting after the postman.
Trotting is moving at a steady pace, quicker than walking.
He kept trotting to keep up with the marching band.

entries.meaning: a state of happiness and satisfaction.
examples: The cat purred with obvious contentment beside the fire.
He found real contentment in his small garden.
There was a look of quiet contentment on her face.
Contentment is a settled feeling of happiness and satisfaction.
Wealth does not always bring contentment.

entries.meaning: a loud and confused noise. Also to demand something noisily.
examples: The clamour of the playground carried across the field.
A clamour of gulls followed the fishing boat into harbour.
Parents began to clamour for a safer crossing outside the school.
Clamour is a loud, confused noise, or a noisy demand.
Above the clamour she could just hear her name.

entries.meaning: so intense that it seems almost able to be touched; clearly noticeable.
examples: The tension in the hall before the results was palpable.
There was a palpable sense of relief when the bus finally arrived.
Excitement in the crowd grew almost palpable.
Something palpable is so strong you can almost touch it.
His disappointment was palpable, though he said nothing.

entries.meaning: diligent and hardworking.
examples: The industrious bees worked from dawn until dusk.
An industrious pupil, she finished the project a week early.
Industrious villagers rebuilt the wall in a single weekend.
Someone industrious works hard and steadily.
His industrious habits made him popular with every employer.

entries.meaning: passing easily or gently through the air.
examples: The smell of fresh bread came wafting from the bakery.
Music was wafting across the garden from an open window.
Blossom went wafting down onto the wet pavement.
Wafting means drifting gently through the air.
A cool breeze came wafting in through the doorway.

entries.meaning: giving out or reflecting small flashes of light.
examples: Sunlight was glinting off the windows of the passing train.
She spotted something glinting among the pebbles.
His glasses kept glinting under the stage lights.
Glinting means giving off small, sharp flashes of light.
The frost lay glinting across the whole playing field.

entries.meaning: repeated several times as an echo; ringing on and on.
examples: Thunder went reverberating around the hills.
The drum's beat was still reverberating through the hall.
Their footsteps came reverberating down the empty corridor.
Reverberating means echoing again and again.
The news went reverberating through the whole village.

entries.meaning: extremely happy, peaceful or picturesque.
examples: They spent an idyllic week in a cottage by the sea.
The village looked idyllic under a light dusting of snow.
Her idyllic childhood was full of long summers outdoors.
Something idyllic is peaceful and almost perfectly lovely.
It was an idyllic spot for a picnic.

entries.meaning: shining with a sparkling light, usually because something is wet.
examples: Dew lay glistening on every blade of grass.
His forehead was glistening after the long race.
The wet cobbles were glistening under the street lamps.
Glistening means shining with a wet, sparkling light.
Glistening icicles hung from the gutter.

entries.meaning: filled with lively energy and excitement.
examples: An exuberant cheer went up as the goal went in.
The exuberant toddler could not sit still for a moment.
Her exuberant painting used every colour in the box.
Someone exuberant is bursting with lively excitement.
Exuberant growth filled the greenhouse by July.

entries.meaning: hazardous or unpredictably dangerous. Also disloyal and not to be trusted.
examples: Black ice made the road treacherous that morning.
The treacherous currents keep swimmers away from the cove.
In the story, a treacherous advisor betrays the queen.
Treacherous means dangerous, or disloyal and untrustworthy.
They picked their way across the treacherous scree.

entries.meaning: the state or quality of being ferocious; savagery.
examples: The storm struck the coast with unexpected ferocity.
The ferocity of the wildcat surprised the photographer.
She argued her case with real ferocity.
Ferocity is fierceness or savage force.
The ferocity of the fire took hold within minutes.

entries.meaning: causing dizziness by being extremely high or steep.
examples: A vertiginous staircase spiralled up inside the tower.
From the vertiginous ledge, the village looked like a toy.
She refused to look down from the vertiginous bridge.
Something vertiginous is so high or steep it makes you dizzy.
The path took a vertiginous turn along the cliff edge.

entries.meaning: affectedly and irritatingly self-important.
examples: The pompous official insisted on being called by his full title.
His pompous speech went on for half an hour.
She used pompous words where simple ones would do.
Someone pompous behaves as though they are far more important than they are.
The character in the play is a pompous but harmless mayor.

entries.meaning: understood or implied without being stated out loud.
examples: There was a tacit agreement that nobody would mention the surprise.
His nod gave tacit approval to the plan.
A tacit understanding grew between the two rivals.
Something tacit is understood without ever being said.
Their silence was taken as tacit consent.

entries.meaning: extremely tiring and demanding.
examples: The team faced a gruelling schedule of five matches in a week.
It was a gruelling climb in the midday heat.
She recovered slowly after the gruelling operation.
Something gruelling is exhausting and very demanding.
The gruelling rehearsals finally paid off on opening night.

entries.meaning: mutual trust and friendship among people who spend time together.
examples: The camaraderie in the changing room was obvious to everyone.
Long expeditions build a special kind of camaraderie.
She missed the camaraderie of her old orchestra.
Camaraderie is the warm friendship shared by a group.
There was real camaraderie among the volunteers.

entries.meaning: causing someone to lose their sense of direction or to become confused.
examples: The thick fog was completely disorienting.
Waking in a strange room can be disorienting.
The hall of mirrors proved wonderfully disorienting.
Something disorienting makes you lose your sense of direction.
She found the sudden change of school disorienting at first.

entries.meaning: sweeping over something so as to surround it completely.
examples: Flames were engulfing the far end of the old barn.
A wave came engulfing the sandcastle they had built.
Fog was engulfing the harbour by late afternoon.
Engulfing means sweeping over something and surrounding it.
A feeling of relief came engulfing her at the finish line.

entries.meaning: relating to earthquakes or other vibrations. Also describing a very great change.
examples: Scientists study seismic activity to predict earthquakes.
The seismic waves were recorded hundreds of miles away.
The invention caused a seismic shift in how people travelled.
Seismic means to do with earthquakes, or hugely significant.
A seismic tremor rattled the windows of the whole street.

entries.meaning: the face, or the appearance of something.
examples: The statue's stern visage stared down at the visitors.
A smile transformed his weathered visage.
The moon's pale visage appeared between the clouds.
A visage is a face or the outward appearance of something.
Her visage betrayed nothing of what she was thinking.

entries.meaning: something that moves around unsteadily. Also a fit of temper.
examples: The loose tooth was a proper wobbler by Friday.
That old table is a wobbler unless you wedge the leg.
He threw a complete wobbler when his tower collapsed.
A wobbler is something unsteady, or a sudden loss of temper.
The fishing lure was a bright wobbler that darted through the water.

entries.meaning: accorded a great deal of respect because of age or character.
examples: The venerable oak has stood in the churchyard for four centuries.
A venerable professor opened the ceremony.
They visited the venerable ruins of the abbey.
Someone venerable is deeply respected for their age or character.
The venerable old ship is now a floating museum.

entries.meaning: courage and resolve; strength of character. Also tiny pieces of stone or sand.
examples: It took real grit to finish the race on an injured ankle.
Lorries spread grit on the roads before the frost.
A piece of grit had worked its way into her shoe.
Grit means courage and determination, but also tiny stones.
He gritted his teeth and carried on to the top.

entries.meaning: a small pit or scar on a surface, typically the skin.
examples: A pockmark on the old table showed where the candle had burned.
Craters pockmark the whole surface of the moon.
The stone wall was pockmarked by years of wind and rain.
A pockmark is a small pit or scar left on a surface.
Rain began to pockmark the smooth sand of the beach.

entries.meaning: the state of being famous or well known for some bad deed.
examples: The highwayman gained notoriety across three counties.
The bend has a certain notoriety among local cyclists.
Her notoriety followed her long after the incident.
Notoriety is fame that comes from doing something bad.
The old prison has a grim notoriety in the town's history.

entries.meaning: having the qualities of surrealism; bizarre or dreamlike.
examples: It felt surreal to see snow falling in the middle of April.
The painting shows a surreal landscape of melting clocks.
There was something surreal about the empty city streets.
Something surreal seems strange and dreamlike rather than real.
Meeting her hero in the supermarket was a surreal moment.

entries.meaning: bad-tempered or difficult to deal with.
examples: The ornery old goat refused to move off the path.
He can be ornery first thing in the morning.
That ornery lawnmower starts only when it feels like it.
Someone ornery is bad-tempered and hard to deal with.
The ornery pony had thrown three riders that summer.

entries.meaning: a person who lives a solitary life and tends to avoid other people.
examples: The writer became a recluse after her final novel.
A recluse had lived in the cottage for thirty years.
He is no recluse, but he does value his quiet evenings.
A recluse is somebody who lives alone and avoids company.
Villagers rarely glimpsed the recluse on the hill.

entries.meaning: a British informal term for a man.
examples: A friendly bloke at the station helped with the suitcases.
My dad is the sort of bloke who fixes everything himself.
Some bloke in a yellow jacket was directing the traffic.
Bloke is an informal British word for a man.
He is a decent bloke once you get to know him.

entries.meaning: to echo or resound. Also to have a continuing effect.
examples: The bells reverberate across the valley every Sunday.
His shout seemed to reverberate around the empty pool.
The decision will reverberate through the club for years.
To reverberate is to echo, or to go on having an effect.
Drums reverberated through the floor of the hall.

entries.meaning: a fictional term meaning to teleport from one place to another.
examples: In the story, the wizard apparated straight into the courtyard.
She apparated away before anyone could stop her.
He wished he could have apparated to school on rainy mornings.
Apparated is an invented word meaning to teleport instantly.
The character apparated with a loud crack and disappeared.

entries.meaning: stitches holding together the edges of a wound or surgical cut.
examples: The nurse removed the sutures a week after the operation.
Six sutures were needed to close the cut on his knee.
Sutures dissolve on their own in some kinds of surgery.
Sutures are the stitches that hold a wound closed.
The vet checked the sutures on the dog's paw.

entries.meaning: worn at the edges or unravelling. Also strained or stressed.
examples: The cuffs of his old jumper were badly frayed.
A frayed rope should never be used for climbing.
Tempers were frayed by the end of the long journey.
Frayed means worn at the edges, or worn down by stress.
She trimmed the frayed ends of the ribbon.

entries.meaning: a person or thing used to mislead or lure someone into a trap.
examples: The wooden duck was a decoy floating among the reeds.
One player acted as a decoy while the other took the ball.
The parcel was a decoy to draw the thieves away.
A decoy is something used to lure or mislead somebody.
Birds will sometimes decoy a predator away from the nest.

entries.meaning: to prevent something from working or succeeding; to sabotage.
examples: A puncture threatened to scupper their whole cycling trip.
Bad weather scuppered the plans for the summer fair.
One careless remark could scupper the entire agreement.
To scupper something is to ruin its chances completely.
He would not let a broken string scupper his performance.

entries.meaning: the past participle of "tread"; walked upon.
examples: They followed a well-trodden path through the woods.
Somebody had trodden mud right across the clean floor.
The grass was trodden flat where the tent had stood.
Trodden means walked upon, and is the past participle of tread.
Few explorers had trodden that part of the island.

entries.meaning: not showing proper respect; rude and cheeky.
examples: It was impertinent of him to interrupt the head teacher.
She asked an impertinent question about his age.
The impertinent reply earned him a detention.
Someone impertinent is rude and shows no proper respect.
He apologised for his impertinent behaviour at the meeting.

entries.meaning: a feeling of smug or uncritical satisfaction with yourself.
examples: An early lead led to complacency and a late equaliser.
The coach warned the squad against complacency.
Complacency about safety checks can be dangerous.
Complacency is being so satisfied that you stop trying.
Her complacency vanished the moment she saw the exam paper.

entries.meaning: a device used by musicians that gives a regular tick to mark time.
examples: She practised her scales in time with the metronome.
The metronome ticked steadily on top of the piano.
His teacher set the metronome a little faster each week.
A metronome is a device that ticks out a steady beat.
The drummer's timing was as reliable as a metronome.

entries.meaning: a short, sharp cry, especially of pain or alarm.
examples: The puppy gave a yelp when it trod on a thistle.
She let out a yelp as the cold water hit her.
A sudden yelp from the garden made everyone look up.
A yelp is a short, sharp cry of pain or surprise.
He yelped and dropped the hot dish onto the worktop.

entries.meaning: to confuse or perplex someone completely.
examples: The last riddle managed to flummox the entire class.
Complicated timetables always flummox him.
She was flummoxed by the instructions for the new camera.
To flummox somebody is to leave them completely confused.
The unexpected question flummoxed even the teacher.

entries.meaning: having a sharply strong taste or smell.
examples: The pungent smell of onions filled the kitchen.
Blue cheese has a wonderfully pungent flavour.
A pungent cloud of smoke drifted from the bonfire.
Something pungent has a sharp, powerful taste or smell.
She wrinkled her nose at the pungent aroma of the compost heap.

entries.meaning: to fill something tightly. Also to study intensively over a short period.
examples: He tried to cram every book into one small bag.
Do not cram your revision into the final night.
They managed to cram eleven people into the minibus.
To cram is to pack tightly, or to study hard at the last minute.
She crammed the last of the leaves into the sack.

entries.meaning: to laugh quietly in a disrespectful or mocking manner.
examples: It is unkind to snigger when someone makes a mistake.
A snigger ran along the back row of the classroom.
They began to snigger at his old-fashioned coat.
To snigger is to laugh quietly in a mocking way.
She heard a snigger and turned round sharply.

entries.meaning: a strong ringing sound made by plucking a string. Also a distinctive accent.
examples: The guitar string gave a loud twang as it snapped.
He plucked the elastic band and made it twang.
There was a slight Yorkshire twang in her voice.
A twang is the ringing sound of a plucked string.
The bowstring twanged and the arrow was gone.

entries.meaning: to travel across or through something.
examples: It took three days to traverse the mountain range.
A narrow bridge allows walkers to traverse the gorge.
The explorers traversed the ice field in single file.
To traverse is to travel across or through a place.
Ants traverse enormous distances relative to their size.

entries.meaning: attractively unusual or old-fashioned.
examples: A quaint tea room sat at the end of the harbour wall.
The village keeps the quaint tradition of well dressing.
He collects quaint old postcards of seaside towns.
Something quaint is attractively old-fashioned or unusual.
Her quaint way of speaking made the story charming.

entries.meaning: a symbol (*) used in text to indicate a footnote or an omission.
examples: An asterisk beside the price warned of an extra charge.
Put an asterisk next to any word you cannot spell.
The asterisk directs the reader to a note at the bottom.
An asterisk is the little star symbol used in writing.
She marked her favourite poems with a small asterisk.

entries.meaning: neatly trimmed or carefully maintained.
examples: The manicured lawns stretched right down to the lake.
Her manicured nails gleamed under the lights.
Neatly manicured hedges lined the driveway.
Something manicured is neatly trimmed and carefully kept.
The manicured cricket square was the groundsman's pride.

entries.meaning: thin, supple and graceful in movement.
examples: The lithe gymnast twisted easily through the hoop.
A lithe cat slipped between the railings.
Years of dancing had made her wonderfully lithe.
Someone lithe is slim, supple and moves gracefully.
The lithe otter slid soundlessly into the river.

entries.meaning: to wriggle the body from side to side because of nervousness or discomfort.
examples: The toddler began to squirm in the uncomfortable seat.
His awkward question made her squirm.
Worms squirm away as soon as the soil is turned.
To squirm is to wriggle about from nerves or discomfort.
He squirmed with embarrassment as the photograph appeared.

entries.meaning: a thing said or done for amusement; a joke.
examples: He said it in jest, but nobody laughed.
Her jest about the burnt toast lightened the mood.
Do not jest about something so serious.
A jest is something said or done to make people laugh.
The court jester's every jest had to please the king.

entries.meaning: walking doggedly and slowly with heavy steps. Also slow and dull in style.
examples: The tired walkers came plodding down the last hill.
A carthorse went plodding along the towpath.
The story was rather plodding until the final chapter.
Plodding means walking slowly and heavily, or being slow and dull.
He kept plodding on until the whole field was dug.

entries.meaning: a fierce or angry stare. Also a strong, harsh light.
examples: She gave him a furious glare across the table.
The glare of the low sun made driving difficult.
He tried not to glare at the boy who had pushed in.
A glare is an angry stare or a harsh, dazzling light.
They shaded their eyes against the glare off the snow.

entries.meaning: serving as a temporary substitute; sufficient for the time being.
examples: They built a makeshift shelter from branches and a groundsheet.
An upturned crate served as a makeshift table.
The hall became a makeshift hospital during the flood.
Something makeshift is a temporary substitute for the real thing.
He made a makeshift repair with tape until the part arrived.

entries.meaning: to make a gesture to tell someone to come towards you. Also to seem attractive or inviting.
examples: She raised her hand to beckon the waiter over.
He beckoned the class into the hall with a nod.
The summer holidays seemed to beckon from the far side of June.
To beckon is to signal to someone to come to you.
The lit windows of the cottage beckoned to the tired walkers.

entries.meaning: to be absorbed in thought. Also a person who inspires an artist.
examples: He sat by the window to muse on the day's events.
She would often muse aloud about becoming an astronaut.
The painter called his sister his muse.
To muse is to be lost in thought about something.
They mused over the strange message for hours.

entries.meaning: a confused mixture of different things.
examples: His bedroom was a hotchpotch of books, socks and models.
The building is a hotchpotch of several different styles.
Supper was a hotchpotch of whatever was left in the fridge.
A hotchpotch is a confused mixture of odds and ends.
Her notes were a hotchpotch that nobody else could follow.

entries.meaning: to say something suddenly and without careful consideration.
examples: Try not to blurt out the answer before the others have thought.
He blurted the secret before he could stop himself.
She blurted an apology and hurried from the room.
To blurt is to say something suddenly, without thinking.
In his excitement he blurted the whole story at once.
